speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since it would appear likely that this will be the last day we will meet before the adjournment until November, and in view of the reported statements by the Prime Minister of Australia in regard to the desirability of holding a commonwealth conference, as well as another statement from London, I wonder if the Prime Minister could not give some assurance that Canada will consider extending an invitation, having regard to the fact that Canada's position is a peculiarly favourable one to indicate a willingness to explore this possibility.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I do not think there is any probability of Canada taking the initiative in the near future. The hon. member knows that these stories are not without some background, but I am not at liberty to discuss any details at this moment. I think any initiative taken by Canada at this time might be a serious embarrassment to those who have already taken initiative to bring about this kind of conference.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Arising out of the reply to the leader of the opposition just made by the Prime Minister, is it not a fact that departmental officials are now gathering information preparatory to a conference to be held in November? Is there not something like that going ahead at the very moment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: There is information being gathered for the purpose of making it available to those who are considering the calling of a conference at a not too distant date. The Canadian government has expressed its desire to co-operate to the fullest possible extent and to make whatever information can be gathered here available for consideration in that connection.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I do not want to enlarge this matter because we must not extend it into a debate, but in view of what has been said
and the desire we all have that everything be done to advance a meeting of this kind I would most earnestly hope that Canada, with its peculiarly favourable position in relation to the commonwealth and the United States, will consider giving every possible lead in this direction that can be given.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
When we had a discussion last night with reference to this matter the hon. member for Greenwood asked several questions which I will attempt to answer at this time. As reported at page 4227 of Hansard for July 3, he said:
First of all I should like to know what the minister considers was the loss to the treasury last year from smuggling operations. He will recall what the Minister of Finance said . . .
The only answer I can give to that question is that nobody knows with any degree of accuracy what that loss was. It can only be an estimate and I would hesitate to make any estimate of what the loss has been in dollars and cents. The hon. member also said:
I do want, however, to get from the minister what he considers the most significant facts. First of all I want to know the number of prosecutions and seizures which were being made prior to the change in the tax on April 8 last, and whether the minister has reason to think the situation has improved very greatly. Some opinions I have heard, though I cannot profess to have verified them, seem to indicate that the change is not nearly as great as one might expect.
I will give the hon. member the information with reference to seizures and perhaps that will suffice to answer the question. Cigarettes seized in the fiscal year 1951-52 amounted to 14,375,891. As against that from April 1, 1952, to May 31, 1952, cigarettes seized amounted to 2,633,932. With respect to prosecutions, for the fiscal year 1951-52 completed prosecutions numbered 508 and those convicted numbered 498. From April 1, 1952, to May 31, 1952, there were 122 completed prosecutions and 117 convictions. The

Supply-National Revenue number of motor vehicles forfeited for carrying smuggled goods in the fiscal year 1951-52 was 152, and from April 1, 1952, to May 31, 1952, the number was 27. In that period there were 41 cases still pending.
I think perhaps I should put on the record the answer to the question of the hon. gentleman as to cigarettes seized by both police and ports for the years 1951 and 1952. I shall give first the 1952 seizures for the months of January to May inclusive. The figures are as follows:

In the whole year 1951 there were 11,080,291 cigarettes seized. The trend of the figures through July, August, September and October and reaching a high point in November indicates to me personally that smugglers of course always operate under cover if they can. In November the hours of darkness are longer which makes it easier for the smuggler to carry on his operations. Of course I think there is always going to be smuggling of cigarettes as long as there is a differential between the price at which they can be purchased in the United States and the price at which they are on sale in Canada. I will not deny that.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Could I ask the minister a question? Before the minister makes his general observations, I am wondering if he is going to give me the figure I asked for particularly last night. That was not the number of cigarettes seized but the number of seizures, that is to say, the number of cases of law-breaking. I said last night that seemed to me the most indicative figure. It is that figure that I should like to get particularly, and all the more because I notice that the prosecutions-and I would be interested to know why-seem to be only a small fraction of what I understand to be the number of seizures.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Is this for cigarettes?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: This is all seizures.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I said last night that as long as we get a comparable figure we can carry the thing right through. Last night the minister gave me some figures for cigarettes and then said later that they were the figures for everything. What I am interested in is getting a comparable figure that can be carried right through.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I doubt if it is possible to give a comparable figure. I say that for the reason that so far as a great many seizures are concerned there might be one carton oi cigarettes, a pair of boots, a tire in a trunk and something else. You could not put that down merely as a seizure of cigarettes, but it is a seizure.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: As long as we get a comparable figure I think that is the best that can be done, but I should like a comparable figure throughout.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:

Starting in January the total number of seizures were: January, 426; February, 421; March, 457; April, 514; May, 600; June, 617; July, 587; August, 680; September, 731; October, 697; November, 687; December, 644. I can give you the totals in 1951 of cigarettes involved-the number of cigarettes that were seized.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
On the
figures the minister has given, as I took them down, the figures for 1952 show no lessening. The figures for 1952 run along practically parallel with those of 1951. I do not want to labour this and spend a lot of time on it but the minister says there is a peak from which we are receding.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think that might be explained by the fact that there is an extra effort and more vigilance on the part of the police in making seizures- and on the part of the department too.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: We can give those figures. I think perhaps the most recent ones might be given first. In 1952 the total number of seizures in January was 559.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: One other question. If I took the figures down correctly the number of prosecutions for 1951-52 was only 508.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Less than the seizures for one month.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Of course, the explanation is that there is not a prosecution in every case.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is certainly clear but I do want to know just the basis, if the minister can indicate it, on which we prosecute such a small number. There is probably some reason that I do not know of, but I would like to know it, and I would like to know also whether the minister thinks the deterrents are strong enough; because the picture one gets is disturbing. I read an estimate, and the figure is probably just plucked out of the atmosphere, but the estimate was that the police are only getting about five per cent. No doubt that is somebody's guess but there is a great deal going on which is not caught.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, for the hon. gentleman's information, we prosecute the people whom we classify as commercial smugglers-those are the people who are definitely known to be in the business; but there is not a prosecution of the odd person who comes along and has a few cigarettes. The cigarettes may be confiscated and that is probably the end of it. If people wish to pay duty and penalty on them, well and good; that is done and that ends the case. If they do not, the cigarettes are confiscated and distributed to veterans' hospitals throughout the country.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
In other
words, you distinguish between professionals and enthusiastic amateurs. I am not going to 'comment further at the moment but I would like to ask a question on this. Just what does the minister consider to be the experience of his department as to the adequacy of the deterrents? This thing is keeping on and it is an ugly business. Has the minister any view to express?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I think that the deterrents have been in a measure fairly effective in that they are helping to stop the big smuggling. Seizures have been made where a truck is seized and on it there is a load of cigarettes worth anywhere from $10,000 to $15,000. Now, we are not finding as much of that because when that truck is seized with $14,000 or $15,000 of cigarettes, and those concerned have to pay a fine, if there is a deterrent at all that is it. I think it is having its effect.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
The minister will recall I think the representations of the tobacco industry particularly last year as to
Supply-National Revenue the damage they were suffering. Is there any indication from them of their feeling about the present situation, whether it has improved, and if so, how much?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I might say that we have not had protest from the industry to the same extent this year. There were other factors in the lessened production figures last year and I refer particularly to the strike in the Imperial Tobacco Company. I do not think that the manufacturers of cigarettes are suffering very much because all indications are that .the total number of domestic cigarettes, Canadian cigarettes made and entered for consumption, is on the increase. For instance, in May of this year consumption was 1,750,711,685 while the consumption in February was only 1,098,023,345. One of the factors entering into that increase is that the budget in April reduced the tax to a degree at least and consumption has increased. Although I do not know that the hon. member for Greenwood appreciated or caught my point, I said last night that there was a great increase in the use of manufactured tobacco. It indicated that an awful lot of people, instead of using and buying tailor-made cigarettes, were making their own. Lately, in the last year or two at least, there has not been a tax on cigarette papers and a lot of people have found it more economical to manufacture their own cigarettes. But, on the whole, there has been an increase in the consumption of tailor-made cigarettes, and I think I can say that there has been less protest from the Canadian manufacturers of cigarettes.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I have just one more question on this point. Who is responsible for the border patrol? Has the department an enforcement branch of its own or does it call in the R.C.M.P. and direct the R.C.M.P,, or vice versa? Who is responsible? Also, to what extent has the patrol force been increased?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Since 1932 the R.C.M.P. have been doing the patrol work for the Department of National Revenue.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Yesterday, I believe, the minister when referring to the increased estimates said that $1,900,000 odd was for salaries-increased salaries. I wonder if he would tell us whether this amount is attributable to raises in salaries or whether it is additions to staff; and possibly he would also comment on the policy of the department with respect to the dismissal of some employees and their replacement with auditors who have degrees?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, as I stated last night the estimates provide for an

Supply-National Revenue increase over last year of $1,999,153 and the larger part, 95 per cent of the $1,999,153, is required to cover adjustments in salaries occasioned by the general increase that was applicable to all government employees. In addition, with respect to the second part of the hon. member's question, part of that sum represents an increase in positions sufficient to bring us up to the same strength we had a year ago. Of course, we are always trying to improve the calibre of the staff but there have not been any releases for the purpose mentioned.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Will the minister state the over-all wage and salary roll of the department?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: There has been an increase of 118 in the salary quota. As of May 31, 1951, we had 4,886 permanents; 1,291 temporaries; and then we have what we call a seasonal staff. The hon. member will understand that in the busy part of the summer we need extra staff. There were 274 of those. This made a total of 6,451. For May 31, 1952, the permanents totalled 5,115. There have been a couple of hundred made permanent, so the temporaries are less, 1,205; seasonal staff is less, 249. This give us a total of 6,569, which is an over-all increase of 118 over the staff of a year ago.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: What is the amount of the total wage roll for the department?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: We provide for $21,608,037; that is the total amount for wages.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Then the increase in wages is almost 10 per cent over last year?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I think he has already been approached on this matter, and it relates to the sales tax imposed on church furniture. In the case of which I am aware, the donor of a gift to a church found that the furniture was marked "sales tax included". Upon making application he found that he had no claim for a rebate of this amount. In the very same church, another donor who had given a stained glass window found that there was no sales tax on those. It seems odd that one type of gift to a church is subject to sales tax and another is not, particularly when they both are classed as gifts to a place of worship.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Church furnishings and
church pews are not exempt from sales tax. If the stained glass windows in this instance were a donation from abroad, we give a remission because usually they are erected as memorials. For instance, if an organ were

erected in a church and had a plaque on it that it was a memorial to those of that congregation who lost their lives in the war, then we make a remission of sales tax.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Would that apply to such things as a reredos, an altar or something of that nature which was given as a memorial? Are they exempt from sales tax?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: No, the exemption has not been extended that far. I presume the hon. member is familiar with the Excise Tax Act, schedule III, in which there are five pages of articles which are exempt from sales tax. A lot of the material that goes into the church -the stone, cement and many other things, the glass for windows-that is exempt from sales tax.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: It seems to me like splitting hairs. I believe that if any of the equipment that goes into a church is exempt, that exemption might very well be extended to cover all the equipment of the church. I do not mean things like portable chairs and so on, but I mean the actual fixtures of the church. I cannot see where the department gains anything by splitting them into classifications and allowing exemption to one group and not another.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is the policy as I have outlined it. I want to indicate to the hon. member that this department is only administrative. If the law is changed and gives further exemptions we shall be very happy to administer the law as indicated in any changes that would be made.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I respectfully suggest that the minister, being the present custodian of policy let us say for the department, should suggest to his colleagues that the law be changed in that respect.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is the rather anomalous and perhaps unhappy situation: we are not policy makers.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
If you cannot make
changes in it, who can?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: We will bring your suggestions to the Department of Finance to see what can be done about them.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I think it is rather odd that a stained glass window as a memorial could be exempt, and we will say a statue in a church or, we will say a reredos, would be taxed. It does not seem to me to be proper. In one instance you have a picture or an image or a reredos containing a number of images, and in one instance sales tax is not imposed while in the other instance it is. It does not seem to me to be sensible.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Well, it is as it is; that is the best answer I can give you.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Did I understand the minister correctly when he said that if a pulpit were erected with a plaque on it saying that it was donated in memory of the men who had fallen in one of the great wars, that was tax free, but if a similar pulpit were erected as a memorial to some private individual or family, it would be taxed?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I was not speaking about pulpits or altars, but about organs.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I am asking about the other.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
The exemption is for
memorials or monuments, and those are exempt under the Excise Tax Act. It must be memorials or monuments erected to members of the armed forces who lost their lives in the service of their country. If an altar or pulpit were erected as a memorial, and it were so indicated, that would be given consideration for exemption and it might qualify.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: A memorial to members of the armed forces?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is what it says, a memorial or monument erected to any members of the armed forces who lost their lives in the service of their country.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That narrows it.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: In other words, it does not apply to a memorial put up to private individuals?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I should like to ask a question about the temporary employees. I noticed the minister gave a figure of 1,291 for temporaries. Then, he said that this represented a reduction of, I think, around 200 in the temporary staff. I understand that the temporary staff is not entitled to be on the pension plan. Is that correct?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Yes; there was a reduction in temporaries this year, from 1,291 a year ago to 1,205; that would be a difference of 86.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
My second question is this. Having regard to my understanding that these people may not be on the pension plan, I would be interested to know just what the situation is with regard to this 1,291. For example, I would be interested in knowing how many of them have been years in the service. In other words, those who are not temporary in any real sense. Secondly, I would be interested to know what wastage there is. How big a problem is this 1,291? Have we got 1,291 people most of whom have been in the government service for a long time, who would like to be under the pension plan and who cannot be? Or have we got 1,291 55704-267i
Supply-National Revenue who are turning over fairly rapidly or where there is a great deal of wastage?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: As a matter of policy, 10 per cent of our staff outside of ports are temporary. An employee comes into the service and, after certain years of service and satisfaction, he is put on the permanent force. Let me indicate to the hon. member that in May, 1951, we had 4,886 permanents and that number has been increased in a year to 5,115. That is an increase of 229 in a year. I think that is a fair increase from temporary employment or from temporaries to permanents, within that time, relative to the number employed.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I would not want to argue against that statement. It is progress. But I am still left without an answer to my question. Let us take into consideration this number of 1,291. First of all, will the minister say exactly what their position is with regard to pension rights? I may not have stated it quite accurately. In the second place, will he say, for example, how many of those 1,291 have been in the service, let us say, five years?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I am giving the information that we have not many who remain temporaries very long. As the hon. member will understand, the temporary pays into the retirement fund. Then when he becomes a permanent, he pays into the superannuation fund and he gets credit, of course, for the money he has put into the retirement fund. The retirement fund applies to temporaries and the superannuation fund applies to permanents. I am told that there are few of our employees whom it takes longer than one, two or three years to be transferred from the temporary force to the permanent force.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That situation sounds fairly satisfactory, but let me ask one further question. When an employee is transferred from the temporary force to the permanent force, as the minister has pointed out, he has had deductions from his salary even during his period as a temporary. Then he becomes permanent and goes under the ordinary civil service plan. Is he in exactly the same position as that in which he would have been if he had been permanent from the time he began to make his payments?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: With regard to superannuation, he is in exactly the same position because he gets that credit.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I am glad to hear that.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I have a matter that I wish to draw to the attention of the minister. If

Supply-National Revenue my understanding is correct, a Canadian who visits the United States for a period longer than 48 hours is allowed to bring back every four months certain things to the value of $100. Is that right?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I had this personal experience myself. A few months ago I visited the United States for ten days, came back and had $19 worth of goods to declare. I was not going over there on a spending spree. I declared that $19 worth of goods, and was immediately told that I would not be able to bring any more goods in from the United States until the four-months period was up. I do not think this is fair. If that is the policy, it encourages people who visit the United States to go the limit. In my case, as I say, I was on no spending spree. I declared this $19 worth of goods that I brought back, and I was immediately told that I would not be able to bring in any more goods tax-free for a four-months period. Is that the policy?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman understands the situation correctly and was given the correct information. It would be an impossible administrative and bookkeeping job if the situation were otherwise. I think I know what the hon. member has in mind. He brought in $19 worth of goods. I think it is his opinion that on another occasion he ought to be able to bring in $131 worth of goods or at least the difference between-

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Is the limit $150 or $100.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: $100. The hon. member thinks he should be able to bring in the other $81 worth?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That would not be in accordance with the law.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I am merely stating that I consider the strict law as being extremely unfair.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: I see what the hon. member means.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: It encourages people to go the limit and to fill the car full.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is a matter that can be given consideration. I do not know Whether any change will be made.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVITATION BY CANADA TO COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I want to raise a matter that I had hoped I might be raising before this time, but this seems to be the only time when I can present it. I do so in the hope that the situation may be given consideration. I am dealing with a particular application that was made for service with this department. Sometimes it is only by dealing with individual

cases that it is possible to make an argument for reconsideration of the general policy. I am mentioning the case of a veteran of the last war by the name of Paul Flewwelling who served with the Royal Canadian Air Force and won the D.F.C. After four years' service with the R.C.A.F., in the bomber command, he returned to Canada. Like a great many other air force veterans he found that he could not become attached here and he went to Britain in 1947 to serve with the R.A.F. He returned in 1951, being unable to get a long term appointment with the R.A.F., in spite of the fact that he had been an instructor and had a high standing as a flying officer with the R.C.A.F. He then applied for a position with the department of customs and excise in Saint John. He wrote the civil service examinations in Saint John in December of 1951. He was informed that he had passed those examinations, but in January of this year he was told by the selection board that he could not get the position in any event because he had not been in the country for one year. He was informed by letter that he had passed the examinations but he was told orally that he could not get the appointment in any event for this reason.
This young man was born sixteen miles from Saint John. They have property there, and during the time that he was in England his wife held that property at all times while he was serving. I raise this point, and I shall be happy to give this young man's address and any other details to the minister or to anyone in the department because it seems to me that this represents one of those cases where regulations made for one purpose produce a result that was never intended. I feel sure that when there is a provision that someone will not be allowed to serve because he has not been in the country a year, it is obviously intended to apply to those who are strangers to Canada, and who are coming to Canada. Of course it is appropriate that persons should spend some time here, which would indicate that they were fitting into our general pattern of life, before they should be taken into the civil service and have to do with matters where they accept some responsibility in relation to the public. I feel, however, that that provision never could have been intended to apply to a young man who was born here and who spent all his life here except for the period that he served in forces that were associated with ours in a common cause.
I raise this now for two reasons: one, to deal with this as a specific case, and the other to use that specific case to express the hope that there will be a re-examination of some of these provisions so that any cases that are affected by service which really is

in the common cause and within the empire shall not deprive anyone of an opportunity for appointment to which he would have been entitled had he remained in Canada at the time, or in a Canadian uniform. This simply happened to be a case where, not being able to serve in a Canadian uniform in that branch of the service for which he was qualified, he joined the Royal Air Force and served in what after all is a common cause.

The actual number of persons with the division at the present time is somewhat short of the number required and a limited number of employees with the requisite qualifications are being engaged through the civil service commission. The total staff required by the division for all district offices as well as at head office should be closer to 7,500 than the present number. However, in conformity with the division's policy of restricting the personnel engaged to those whose qualifications are best suited to the work, it is unlikely that this figure will be reached for some time. The average


monthly salary of all persons employed by the division at 1st May, 1952, was $252 as compared with $242 a year ago.
The next item to which I would like to refer is travelling expenses. The estimate for this year provides for a total of $700,000 which is $92,000 less than the estimate for last year. The department, in co-operation with the office of the comptroller of the treasury, scrutinize the travelling expenses very carefully and ensure that such are incurred only where warranted. Hon. members will appreciate that in the work of the division the part represented by the examination of records in the field is very important. For this reason it is essential that officials of the division do a good deal of their work in the field.
The third largest item in the estimates this year is for postage in the district offices. This item is $600,000 as compared to $650,000 provided for 1951-52.

A closely related item for which an increased estimate is provided is office machine equipment. The amount this year is $142,500 as opposed to $35,000 last year. The increase in this item is occasioned by the acquisition of modern accounting machines and reproducing equipment which will be used in dealing with the accounts of employers deducting the tax at source from their employees. The revised procedure which has been developed effects substantial staff economies throughout the district offices and, in addition, achieves a more efficient bookkeeping system which should be of assistance to employers in their dealings with the district offices. The highest order of efficiency and service is warranted in accounting by the division for the taxes deducted by employers when one considers that through this source of revenue alone something like $800 million in taxes is collected. The revised system has been installed and is operating in several district offices.

On many occasions in the past I have brought to the attention of the house the question of taxation as it applies to farmers. We had intended to have quite a discussion but because the estimates of the Department of National Revenue have not been brought in until this late date it will have to be postponed until another time.


There is, however, a new brand of confiscation that has been imposed on farmers, and I have a letter concerning a particular case which was written by the lady concerned on the same date this session opened. I believe we discussed this matter to some extent at the time the budget resolutions were before the house. At that time I took up with the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance the question of bachelors not being able to receive an exemption for wages paid to housekeepers. At that time the parliamentary assistant thought it was quite a joke and he said that perhaps the farmer should marry the housekeeper. However, if some of the farmers concerned had attempted to pick a wife for the parliamentary assistant perhaps he would not have thought it was quite so much of a joke.
I think this matter deserves consideration because after all farmers are natural people. Every bachelor farmer has his work to do on his farm and I think he is entitled to exemption for the wages paid to a housekeeper, but up to the present time that has been denied. I believe that farmers are as much entitled to lead a natural life in every sense of the word as anybody else, but in the light of the circumstances which I intend to relate in a moment it will be apparent that they are not supposed to live that way.
The case I am concerned with at the present time has to do with a farmer and his wife. Apparently they did the natural thing some years ago and were married legally. The farmer was a man of small means. In my case when I came to this country I had $50 and when I got married I was in debt to the tune of a few thousand dollars. In this case the farmer's wife had owned some cattle before her marriage, and after they were married they naturally put their herds together and went to work as many of us did on our farms in the earlier days, and as I expect is being done at the present time. After some time the lady's herd of cattle increased, as did her husband's, and they were able to purchase a half section of land. However, the time came when ill health and general conditions compelled them to reduce their herds. They did so and apparently placed the proceeds of the sale in the bank in the husband's name but the wife had a power of attorney.
In 1948 a government annuity contract was purchased to yield the wife $100 a month as soon as she reached the age of 60, and I might say that in a very short time she will have reached that age. That policy cost them $13,268.76. The purchase was made out of the proceeds of the sale of their basic

livestock herd on which the income tax department had been satisfied so far as income tax was concerned. It was their money to do with as they pleased. If they had had a joint account, as many farmers and their wives do, and the lady had signed the cheque in payment for the annuity I do not suppose any trouble would have arisen in connection with the matter. However, because the husband signed the cheque we find that after a little while they received a notice of assessment from the taxation division at Edmonton indicating that they owed gift tax amounting to $1,184.63. The gift tax was assessed because the farmer had signed the cheque for the purchase of the annuity.
I do not believe they had any ulterior motive because they have not got very much property, but it was pointed out to them by the taxation division at Edmonton that it was one method of evading succession duty. At the time they purchased the annuity they were advised by the annuity office in Edmonton that there would be no tax on the transaction simply because they had already paid income tax on the amount received from the sale of their basic herd. However, they were assessed the sum of $1,184.63 and that amount has been confiscated from them in the Russian manner. That is not the way to increase production in this country. They and many other farmers have curtailed their production drastically because of the taxation methods employed. I believe such methods should not be tolerated by this or any other government.
Earlier in the session I took the matter up with the minister and had most courteous replies from him but we did not get a refund of the amount. I believe a refund with interest should have been made long before now. The amount should never have been collected to begin with. The result is that the annuity contract has cost these people $14,453.39 for an annuity of $100 per month. The policy is only guaranteed for ten years. The lady says that because of the state of her health she doubts very much whether she will reach the age of 70 but if she does she will have collected $12,000. It appears to me that there is something wrong. It would seem that there is a penalty because people live a natural life.
I am not accusing the minister of dishonesty, far from it. I have known him since 1935 and I have a lot of respect for him. However, I also know the farmers of the west, having lived there since 1914, almost forty years. I know the struggle that many young people have had in order to make a living, and now when they have reached a 55704-223
Supply-National Revenue certain age and their health is broken simply because of the conditions under which they have had to live, in what is a semi-arid part of the province along the south line of my constituency, they are treated in this way by the Department of National Revenue. I feel that it is not good enough and I am asking now that, without further delay, the Department of National Revenue refund those people the amount of $1,184.63 plus 6 per cent interest; because that is the amount the government would have charged them had they not paid their income tax.

There are two or three things I should like to mention to the minister at this time. In the first instance I would like to ask him when he is replying to give us some information about when we may expect the regulations regarding deferred capital cost allowance will be withdrawn. At the time those regulations were put into effect there were some restrictions on building, and supplies were not available. It was thought advisable to curtail investment in both building and equipment, but as conditions have eased somewhat, and as this particular regulation causes a considerable amount of difficulty from the standpoint of both accounting in the various establishments concerned and, I am sure, within the department itself, I hope that serious consideration will be given to withdrawing those regulations within the course of the current year.
The minister spoke a few moments ago about the time limit for the making of appeals. In that regard I might say that the government treats the taxpayer in a manner entirely different from that in which he is allowed to act himself. I have particular regard to investigations which have been made within the last couple of years. The main complaint I have had was from a professional man, a doctor, and I will use his case to illustrate.

In this instance the officials went into his office and went back not for one year or two years or three years but for ten years. I am sure that the minister, himself would have difficulty remembering details of operations in his office ten years ago. I know that I would myself. I do not think I can remember matters of administration within my office three years ago. If anyone asked me, unless I had a complete record on paper I am sure I could not answer any questions. I believe a busy professional man suffers considerable injustice when investigations are conducted over such a long period. I realize that during the war with the added work in the department and the difficulty of obtaining staff there was a backlog of work and examinations of returns were not completed for sometimes four or five years. But at the present time I think it is pretty well caught up-or that is the information I have; and I do not believe it is right that there should be no time limit on these investigations. If the department has not caught up with the taxpayer withih four or five years it does not seem fair that they should go back for that length of time unless there is quite a bit of evidence of failure to report income. Where a man has reported right along and has paid his tax it does not seem proper to me that the department, merely for the sake of checking his records, should go back ten years. In the particular case to which I have reference, when the investigation was over there had not been anything to speak of, and it does not seem proper.
Earlier in this session I spoke with regard to the method employed in the department for computing dependents' allowance with particular reference to children who are eligible for family allowances and those who are not. At that time I put a case on the record where a child did not qualify by reason of residence until December, and the parent of that child was only permitted to charge a $150 exemption. If my memory serves me well, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance at that time took up the question and said: Well, in any event, in the year in which the allowance ceased, that is the year in which the child became 16 years of age, the guardian or parent would benefit to the extent of being allowed the full $400 exemption despite the fact that the child was eligible for only a portion of the year.
In that case, peculiarly enough, they only received family allowance for two months- December in the one year and January in the next. I became interested in this case and wrote back to find out whether or not they did receive any allowance at all for December and I found that while they were

required to deduct only $150 for this dependent they did not even receive family allowances in the December in which the child qualified. In the following month, January of the following year, they received a cheque for two months-for December in the one year and for January of the next year-and that was the end of it. It arises out of the current policy of the federal income tax department in attempting to tax what is usually called the reserve for unredeemed tickets of dairy, bakery and other businesses using tickets as a payment convenience for themselves and 55704-268i
Supply-National Revenue their customers. In some cases these amounts for unredeemed tickets have been set up on the company's books as reserves. I admit that the term "reserve" is really a misnomer when applied to all these tickets. This term may be the chief cause of the present trouble. It may be that a more acceptable accounting practice would be to credit the proceeds of tickets sold to an account named "liability for unredeemed tickets" or "customers' deposits on future sales." Then, when the goods or services were delivered and some tickets redeemed, they could enter the amount of the goods delivered as a sale, with a consequent reduction in the aforesaid liability account.
In computing taxable income, it is stated in the Income Tax Act, section 12 (1) (e), that no deduction from taxable income shall be allowed in respect of an amount transferred or credited to a reserve, contingent account, or sinking fund except as expressly permitted by this part. It can be argued that if the sales of tickets are not credited to income in the first place, it is not necessary to claim them as deductions. Moreover, if the proceeds of tickets are credited to a liability account not called by the term "reserve", it can be contended that the above subsection of the act does not apply to it.
I think it might be well to consider the relationship of this problem to some other industries, because some businesses require deposits on account of a customer's order for goods before they will proceed to work on or supply goods. For instance, in the case of a big machine ordered, a manufacturer may require a large deposit to help finance the cost of manufacture or to guard against a substantial loss if the customer does not accept delivery when the machine is completed. A rental may be prepaid, let us say, over a period of a year or a retaining fee received for work to be done in the succeeding year or a customer's accidentally overpaid balance may be left to apply on account of the next periodic purchase. All the foregoing represent payment received in advance of goods or privileges to be delivered, and the income tax department does not require them to be assessed as taxable income. They can be set up on the company's or individual's books and claimed as deferred. It does not require contractors to pay on profits until the contracts are completed. Why then does it require dairies and bakeries, transportation companies and so on, to pay on receipts for which they have not yet bought the goods to make delivery? I claim, Mr. Chairman, this is discrimination.

A very important point to be considered is that a real liability for a cash refund on tickets does exist. I have never heard of any dairy or bakery, and I am sure the minister has not either, which has refused to return cash on demand for any tickets presented to it. Just recently in Hamilton, as a matter of fact within the last couple of months when the Hamilton street railway issued new tickets at an increased rate it advertised particulars of, and actually carried out, a redemption of the old unused tickets in the hands of customers. The drivers for dairies and bakeries carry cash and tickets on the same basis, and they are equivalent in value, and equivalent to each other in making their returns at the end of the day when accounting for the day's sales. In practice, all the time they are giving cash on demand for tickets. Whether or not there is a legal liability to redeem in cash, so far as I know this practice has been followed in winding up or bankruptcy proceedings.
Businesses with a liability for outstanding tickets appearing on their financial statements, Mr. Chairman, are approached by the income tax assessors in the first place, and asked if they will accept an assessment on their ticket liability account. If so, they are offered the proposition that the full balance of the said liability may be added to the taxable income of the enterprise for the year 1949, or else may be spread over the years 1949 to 1951 in any reasonable proportion which can be substantiated by figures submitted by the taxpayer. If the taxpayer will not accept this proposition or indicates that he will appeal on principle to the appeal board, which he has a legal right to do, then the department will withdraw its proposition and assess the ticket liability account on the basis of increases in it for the full period from six years prior to the date of the last assessment to the present time. It will also charge interest-'there again we have a contentious point, Mr. Chairman-on those reopened assessments of prior years. This reopening of these old assessments often goes back to 1944 or 1943 affecting periods when the 75 per cent and 100 per cent excess profits taxes were in force, and resulting in very large additional bills for income and excess profits taxes. In those years the taxpayer had no inkling of any such treatment by the income tax department, and frequently the assessments are staggering to their financial position. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the whole approach indicates strong-arm methods, with the use of a particularly heavy club to discourage appeals.

Canada's shortwave service continues its work of interpreting Canada and its policies to the world. This is an increasingly important work. Canada is also bearing its share in the positive and intelligent presentation of the free world's position in the current struggle for the minds of men.
The work of this service in the world arena has great psychological, political and economic significance. It is a source of solid encouragement to all men who continue to believe in the democratic way of life; and there are many listeners-perhaps more than we may at times imagine-who do so under the most adverse circumstances. It is an untrammelled source of information that respects no frontiers, recognizes no iron curtains. With a twist of the listener's finger, it can fill a hall, hush to a whisper or be silent at a sound on the stairs. It is a source of fact -hard, uncompromising fact-for those who have no other access to fact, access otherwise only to distortion and perversion. And is it not truth which shall make men free? It is a source for knowledge of democratic processes and democratic achievement. And is not Canada a great source of inspiration for us here? Further, by developing a wider knowledge of our country and its resources, its economic and industrial potential and its business world, it serves as a means of conditioning for trade development markets such as Latin America which Canadians are now just beginning to exploit. At a time when people who seek to discuss public affairs are placed under very severe limitations as to their opportunity to discuss them over the radio, at a time when members of parliament are placed under definite limitations, I think it is entirely wrong that those who have expressed such clear political slants should be given such encouragement at public expense to express their views along a straight propaganda line.

speechtext:
This item covers a further loan of $2 million to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to support the development of its television service and to provide for some additional capital expenditures. Members will recall that two and a half years ago, when we made the first loan to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for television development I said that we had to envisage considerable further financing for the Montreal and the Toronto projects. At that time a loan of $4,500,000 for television was made to the C.B.C., followed by a further loan of $1,500,000 in 1950. This total of $6 million already loaned will cover the capital cost of the production centre stations at Montreal and Toronto, and in addition will provide funds to cover other expenditures up to the time of going on the air with regular service.
The corporation expects to be providing regular service for the Montreal and Toronto projects early in September of this year. Through the years the national television service will be supported by the licence fees from those to whom it is available and by additional commercial revenue. The amount and the details of television licence fees are now under consideration and are expected to be announced prior to the inauguration of the regular service.
As I said when the subject first came up in the house, it will be necessary to provide loans to the corporation not only to cover capital installations but also to help to provide service during initial periods when the number of television viewers is building up. These loans are made on a businesslike basis to the corporation. Full interest rates are charged on them and the corporation will have to repay them in the future. As long as this system is maintained no tax money from individuals in Canada to whom the service is not available will be used to provide television service in other areas.
This loan of $2 million will also make it possible for the corporation to begin construction of a television station in the Ottawa area. It will be remembered that the last special committee of the house on broadcasting was told by representatives of the C.B.C. that the corporation would like to proceed as soon as possible with the construction simultaneously of television stations in seven other areas in addition to Montreal and Toronto. They said that a capital cost of some $7 

million would be involved. Loans for capital funds needed have to be provided by the government. The government has carefully considered these proposals and has decided that funds should be provided at the present moment to start only the station for the Ottawa area. By late next spring the network between Montreal and Toronto already should be passing through Ottawa and the operation of a station here will be particularly economical, more so than in any other area. The government is therefore, for the present, authorizing the start of this project.
We believe there is a sound basis in the national interest for a much wider plan covering nationally-owned television facilities in other parts of the country starting, for obvious reasons of economy, in those most heavily populated. We believe that before asking parliament to authorize the necessary loans it would be wise to wait until after the television service of the corporation has started, and it is possible for the public to get a better idea, of what Canadian television service will be. A much wider development of nationally-owned facilities would meet the principles of the Massey commission report, and will give Canadian life and Canadian talent a chance to develop through this new medium. A plan for wider expansion in the western, central and maritime provinces has been by no means rejected, but we think it wise to give the matter further study, in which some knowledge of what the C.B.C. can do at the Montreal and Toronto centres will be of great assistance. Canada will shortly be producing her own television and I think it will be possible to make more sure decisions about the future after the service has started.
Mr. Chairman, I think that outlines as briefly as we could put it the policy of the government with reference to the further development of television. New stations will be opened in Montreal and Toronto in September, and the advances that there have been in television development make it possible by a relay system developed by the Bell Telephone Company to transmit those programs from Montreal and Toronto. It makes it very easy to develop a station here in Ottawa where we expect to spend something in the neighbourhood of $800,000 for a station which will contain a transmitter and which will also have some origination programs.
As far as policy goes that is the extent of the development proposed until the public have had an opportunity of seeing what the development in Montreal and Toronto produces and how well they are satisfied with it.

Mr. Chairman, there is one point in regard to the development of television by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which it seems to me does call for a careful re-examination by the government, and ultimately by the members of this house. I place it before the government at the moment in the hope that there may be reconsideration of this subject.
It seems to me that many of the arguments that can be made to support the spending of a substantial amount of public revenue on the maintenance of ordinary radio broadcasting cannot be made to apply in the same way to television. The minister has indicated that in a short time television will be available in Toronto and Montreal and fairly soon, as a result of a new system developed by the Bell Telephone Company, in Ottawa as well. That is not going to make television available generally throughout Canada.
I think it will be agreed that one of the fundamental ideas behind the set-up of a publicly-owned operating system, as distinguished from a supervisory body, was that it would make it possible to carry radio into every part of Canada and that the ordinary economic factors which might limit the availability of radio in distant areas, if it were carried out entirely by private stations, would be overcome. This does not apply at the present stage to television. Out of public funds contributed by the taxpayers of the whole of Canada television is going to be made available in Toronto, Montreal, and later in Ottawa. The minister has gone so far as to say that the expansion of television facilities in the west and in the mari-times has by no means been rejected. That is not a very optimistic expression of hope that in these areas there will be television.
The fact remains that private stations now operating ordinary radio have sought the right to provide television in areas which have no chance of getting television at an early date or at any reasonably early date if this present policy is adopted. Whatever arguments there may be in favour of the public operation of ordinary broadcasting, it seems to me that wisdom, economy and common sense would suggest that applications by private radio stations to operate television stations should be granted where those stations are ready to carry out the experimental work and to provide programs that otherwise will not be available for years.
Either this is a great modern means of communicating ideas or it is not. Most people think that it is. Most people think that although it is in its early stages it is a
Supply-National Revenue tremendously powerful means of influencing people's thoughts and of giving educational possibilities to people by this new and remarkable device. In many parts of Canada, for years to come, television broadcasts are going to be available only from the United States unless the policy is changed. That means that through subtle propaganda to a very considerable extent ideas of life in the United States are going to be permeating or are going to become parts of the thoughts of our people at a time that we are supporting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation particularly for the purpose of developing Canadian thinking along Canadian lines.
I am not criticizing the fact that television broadcasts in the United States have -a very definite propaganda flavour in support of what is done by the United States. It would be unnatural if it were otherwise. I think that in every country these great media of communication naturally extol the virtues of their own country and place before the people of their own .country the developments that are taking place and the achievements of which they have every reason to be proud. For a long time Canadians will be seeing more of achievement in the United States than they will of achievement in Canada at a time when some of the most challenging things are being done in Canada which should be the inspiration of every young Canadian.
When private radio stations are ready to provide television broadcasts over widespread areas which under present policies will not be serviced by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I think it is wrong to deny them that opportunity. By the use of moving picture films and other devices new stations can give television broadcasts in areas that will not otherwise be served and those television broadcasts would be broadcasts with a definite Canadian flavour.
I leave it there. I do not know how it is possible to justify in the minds of the taxpayers of the maritimes, of the prairie provinces, of the distant north and, yes, of a considerable part of Ontario and Quebec as well, the thought that their money shall be collected for the purpose of supplying television broadcasts to these favoured areas while the opportunity to have the television broadcasts that they know they could have from private stations is denied under a policy which I must confess I simply cannot understand.

May I say a word? I think most of the arguments the leader of the

Supply-National Revenue opposition used in favour of permitting private television broadcasting should be used in the opposite direction. As a matter of fact, the production of television programs is very expensive. I have no doubt that films and other programs that would be used by private stations, because they would be relatively cheaper, would be largely United States productions. As a matter of fact, when we speak of films I regret exceedingly that we are so dependent upon Hollywood and the United States for the production of films. From my observations of what has been done in radio, the private stations very largely rely on programs that originate in the United States or upon recordings that come almost exclusively from that country and have a distinctly American flavour.
The hon. member says that this is a great medium of public propaganda, and so it is. I do not think it is safe, in the days in which we live, to allow all the propaganda facilities to be in the hands of private stations or private interests. The House of Commons approved of the establishment of the so-called Massey commission. This commission investigated the matter of television very thoroughly, and we understood when the report was formulated and placed before the house that the probability was that this report would guide parliament and the broadcasting corporation as well as other cultural organizations in the country for a period of at least ten years.
I agree with the hon. member that we should not deny to the other parts of Canada the television facilities that will be available to Montreal and Toronto in the near future. But nonetheless, I think that while we expect the corporation to push ahead with television as rapidly as possible to serve as many communities as possible in Canada, we should bear in mind always that these very important facilities should be used as a means of the encouragement of Canadian education and of Canadian culture. I do not think we could do that if we relied on private stations indulging in commercial advertising. I do not think the United States programs give a good understanding or view of the American way of life. My viewing of television programs in the United States leads me to believe that they are quite inadequate, and often of a very low type, advertising all kinds of things that at least I would not want to see brought into my own home. I think that we should do everything we can to avoid the repetition of what has happened in the United States.
We might take some cognizance of what has been done under the B.B.C. in the United Kingdom. I have no doubt that if television facilities were placed in the hands of private

organizations, in order to make them pay for this very expensive means of entertainment or communication, they would endeavour to use all the hours they could so that the advertising revenue would pay for the facilities. In other words, they would have to operate their television stations most of the day in order to make ends meet. In the United Kingdom there are only certain hours when television is available, and that is because the kind of programs that they are using in the United Kingdom are of quite a different type, in many instances, from the kind of programs we see in the United States. We have the Massey report. The Massey commission went into this matter thoroughly, and investigated the systems in various countries. They made very definite recommendations for our guidance. I think we would do well to follow out the recommendations made by the Massey commission as much as possible, and at the same time encourage the broadcasting corporation by providing the necessary finances to establish television across the country. We should enable them to provide all Canadians, as rapidly as possible, with the opportunity to view television. I do think that we should be careful lest we permit the prostitution of this great new educational facility by the hucksters who advertise their wares over the radio to the annoyance of a large number of people.

I should like to say a few words on this matter, because I think there is much to be said on both sides. I think that the government is to be commended for their cautious approach to television. I am aware that there are many educationists in Canada today who want no part of television. I have heard some of them come out and say that after a few generations of television oui* children will have, like Cyclops, but one eye. I do not think that is any solution. I do not think that we can turn back the clock. I think the only cure for the situation is to provide better programs.
I believe the government is to be commended for being cautious by reason of the cost of bringing television to the Canadian people. I do not think they have convinced the Canadian people adequately or made them aware of the difficulties standing in the way of television for everyone. I think a better job could be done in that line. I commend the minister for making progress in respect to Montreal and Toronto, and I think the entire house will accept his explanation as to why Ottawa was thought of as the third point of development. But 1 want to draw his attention to what is going on in Vancouver today. Anyone who has

read the Massey report would be very apprehensive if he took a look at Vancouver because the invasion is on there today. We have many hundreds of sets which are picking up programs that are beamed from Seattle and from a relay station now located in Bellingham, which is only sixty miles away.
There was a suggestion out there that it should not have been impossible for private stations and the corporation to work together to bring into Vancouver, probably at an earlier date than the corporation could otherwise have done, television programs. I do not share all the misgivings concerning private stations, under proper agreements, that are held by the hon. member who just spoke. But I will agree with him that the product of the invasion from the United States at the present time is, in fairly large part, a pretty shoddy performance.
Just in summing up, I think the minister should acquaint the Canadian people, by some publicity, with the magnitude of the problem and the great extent to which we are trying today to bring distinctly Canadian television programs to the Canadian people. In that regard, I do not think we have done a particularly good job. I think there would be, if it were properly explained, a tendency on the part of the Canadian people to wait.
We have been very fortunate, I am told, in being cautious in that we have avoided the fantastic mists which have been created in the United States owing to the blocking of certain wave lengths. There is much commendation due to the department.
I would ask the minister to give the Vancouver area his early attention. We are there drawing programs which probably could not be available to, let us say, a city like Winnipeg. We have high hills which provide for excellent pick-up. The pick-up from Seattle and I think from Bellingham-although I would not be sure of that-is very good in Vancouver. The American invasion is on and it is something which I think we should do our best to repel.

What I, have to say then has to do not particularly with the act but with its administration. During my years as a member I have had something to do with nearly all the departments of government at one time or another. While all the problems that I have referred to the department of immigration have received courteous attention, the results in every case have been negative.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Never once have I been able to get any good results. There has been delay, procrastination and excuses right down the line. Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the leadership of the Liberal party is in the very best hands and there are a great many people in Canada who hope that it remains that way.

Nevertheless if the minister is going to be judged upon the operations of the department of immigration I am afraid that he is losing favour with a certain number of people. I mention this for his own good; I do not care how he looks at it.
Ordinarily I do not take up a great deal of the time of the committee and this being the last day of the session probably I should apologize, but there are a few cases to which I should like to refer. I have the case of a farmer who wanted to bring out a farmer from his native country. This farmer went back to his native land on a visit and saw this other man. Yet a year and a half later he is still there. One excuse after another has been offered, but he has not been able to come.
What country?

Switzerland. I have under my hand a circular put out by the deputy minister of labour. I do not think this was sent to members of parliament as I think it came to my home. It is addressed to Canadian employers and reads in part as follows:
-one thousand farm workers and 500 other classes, and some farm couples. There are also married couples who would be suitable for farm work and a few families with agricultural backgrounds.


On January 5 I wrote to the department in connection with a farmer who wanted a married couple with three, four or five children of public school age or older. Up to date he has not been able to secure that couple. I was told that they were not available so I went to the trouble of advertising in a German newspaper and I have here twelve applications from suitable families who are anxious and willing to come. There has been nothing but excuses from the department; they were not able to get them. I think that is the complete answer. These families are available if they want to find them. This farmer has a good brick house, a garden, cattle and everything they would need and he operates one of the finest farms in the country. Yet this family was not available.
I have another case here where an application was made early in June 1949, and the negotiations went on-you can see the thickness of the file-until some time in September, 1951. I mentioned this case in committee. At that time I received a letter from a Liberal lawyer saying that I would not need to take any more action in the case because he was taking it up. In December of that same year the immigrant, who had been refused admission because of tuberculosis, was admitted to the country. I can give the name and all the details. Apparently that was the best cure for tuberculosis that could be found, and it was certainly the quickest.
These are things that get under my skin and the public generally do not like them. I would be the first to object to anyone being admitted to the country who could not meet the health requirements. 2.	(a) 3; (b) 1; (c) 4; total 8.
I realize that that may be a correct reply as far as the department is concerned, but it does not give a true picture of what happened because probably many cases are hospitalized and not reported to the department. To back up that statement I have here in my

hand a statement from a very reliable authority that has had to do with some of these cases. I should like to indicate some of the things that I think should be done in order to see that persons coming to Canada are properly examined as far as tuberculosis is concerned.
There should be a most thorough study made of X-rays of the chest. The X-ray film should be at least four inches by five inches, and preferably fourteen inches by seventeen inches. Any suggested lesion in the film should delay the individual coming to Canada until such time as it is felt that there is absolutely no evidence of activity. A miniature film of the chest should be taken within a month following the individual's arrival in Canada. This should be kept for record purposes in a suitable film library. A repeat X-ray of the chest should be taken six months after arrival and possibly a third eighteen months after arrival. These X-rays need be only of the miniature variety. Too often immigrants coming to Canada are lost track of and are not followed up with repeat X-ray films of the chest as they should be. In the case of children, it might be well to have them tuberculin skin tested shortly after arrival in Canada.
While I am dealing with immigration, there is one question that has been mentioned many times before to which I should like to refer. Dominion bureau of statistics figures reveal that during the past ten years 591,000 odd immigrants came to Canada, and that in the same period some 486,000 people left Canada, so that we actually had a net gain of one out of each six who came here.
What years did you quote?
These are figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics, and they show that although 591,000 immigrants entered Canada during the last ten years 486,000 people left during the same period.
What ten years is that?
The ten years previous to 1951.
Whose figures are you quoting?
These are figures that the leader of the opposition used in a speech at Toronto recently.

I thought you were quoting D.B.S. figures.
