They were dominion bureau of statistics figures that he quoted.
I should like to see them.

I think Canadians generally feel that with our vast areas we need more people of the right class. After all, as soon as an immigrant comes to this country he is immediately in the market for all the goods and services that he can purchase. I have said before that it would be far better to have these people in Canada producing wealth of one kind and another than to have them in Europe or elsewhere and have to give food and other things to them. As soon as they come here they become self-supporting and more. With all our great natural resources we can certainly absorb a great number of them. When they come here they become consumers, producers and taxpayers; they will likely have to pay sales tax on the very first item they purchase. They will be consumers of some of the surplus food products that the farmers of Canada are finding it difficult to dispose of at the present time.
One of the difficulties in securing the type of immigrant that we desire is the fact that many people in Europe who would like to come here have a stake in their homeland. They have investments there. They are the ones who would make good citizens here but because of the inconvertibility of exchange they are not able to bring very much of their resources to this country. Consequently they hesitate to leave their homeland where they already have a stake. I wonder if it would not be good policy on the part of the government to make long term loans to such people taking as collateral 25 per cent, 50 per cent, 75 per cent or whatever you like of their holdings in their homeland. Over a period of years it is quite possible that we would accumulate investments in other countries which would be quite an asset to us, especially if our dollar continues to rise. That would enable immigrants to come to this country who have demonstrated a certain amount of ability in their homeland.
I know very well that there are a good many in the British isles and elsewhere who would come here if they were able to bring a good portion of their wealth with them and invest it here. I think it is rather discouraging to many Canadians that the bulk of the emigrants from the United Kingdom are going to Australia, New Zealand and other places rather than to Canada. From the experience I have had in my constituency and elsewhere I do not believe there is anything, with the exception of the cost of

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration living and taxation, that is of more concern to people generally than the question of immigration. In view of what I have said to the minister I hope he will revise his plans and adopt some of the suggestions I have made. I must confess that all the dealings I have had with the department have been discouraging.

I am sorry to
hear my hon. friend say what he has said. Of course I am at a slight disadvantage. He has not done me the favour of referring these particular cases to me either by name or by any other means so that I could identify them. I want to point out to the committee, however, that as he himself admits it is undesirable to admit to this country people suffering from tuberculosis or similar diseases. He cited one case that he said had been before the department for over two years. I take it during that time my hon. friend was seeking to convince the government that they ought to admit that particular immigrant because he did not have tuberculosis, and on pure speculation I would also think that during that time it would be safe to say that the department was writing to my hon, friend and saying that we were taking other X-rays of that particular person and hoping that the results would be more favourable in the future, as has turned out to be the case in the end. Would that be correct?
That is about correct.

Then I suggest my hon. friend was not being entirely fair with the committee in his comments. He also raised the question of obtaining a farm family with a specific number of children. I am sorry that we have not been able to produce a farm family according to those specifications. We do our best, as I think my hon. friend knows. I think he will also agree with me that in the main the farm workers in Ontario are of Dutch and German origin, and that the choice of those who are to be Dutch immigrants lies largely with the Netherlands government as a result of our agreement. Of course we have an interest in their health and other matters. At the same time I must express surprise and disappointment that in the matter of five months we were not able to find a family with the specified number of children for that particular farmer, and if he will again refer the matter to me I shall be delighted to see what I can do, even in the short time we have.
My hon. friend raised two other points. One was that a greater proportion of the immigration should be from the United Kingdom. He may have been present in the house when I said a little over a month ago that

immigration from the United Kingdom was a greater proportion of the total this year. I would ask leave to table a statement of the immigration for the first five months which will indicate that during that time immigration from the United Kingdom rose something in the order of 75 or 80 per cent over the comparable period of 1951. It also indicates that immigration from France rose over 100 per cent, and that immigration from the north European countries is generally up and immigration from other areas generally down.
Finally, my hon. friend referred to some
590,000	immigrants having entered this country and over 480,000 having left. I can only say that I am not aware of the dominion bureau of statistics ever having issued figures of that kind. If he will give me the reference I shall be glad to look into it.

Mr. Chairman, there is a
matter I wish to refer to, and it is this. My mind goes back to April of 1949. There had been a conference of commonwealth prime ministers and I recollect that the Prime Minister of Canada made a statement following the decision of India and the commonwealth countries for her to remain within the commonwealth as an independent republic and he said:
Everyone will rejoice in the fact that, notwithstanding the exercise by the people of India of their right to determine the form of their domestic government, it has been found possible to have India remain a member of the commonwealth and to continue for the peace of the world the association of those nations whose traditions give them the same concept of a proper way of living and of democratic processes designed to further the welfare of the men and women of their respective nations.
That of course was the comment made on the announcement from London in April of 1949 of the association of India with the commonwealth. The declaration read this way:
Accordingly, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, Pakistan and Ceylon hereby declare that they remain united as free-
And I want to draw attention to the next words.
*-and equal members of the commonwealth of nations, freely co-operating in the pursuit of peace, liberty and progress.
That evoked statements by the leader of the opposition, myself, and others in the house expressing our approval both of the statement and of what was involved. I am rising this afternoon to say, as briefly as I can, that while there may be some equality among the component parts of the commonwealth as countries Canada is not according to the citizens of all the commonwealth countries associated with her equal status as

individuals when it comes to immigration. I think it is a matter of some concern that considerable dissatisfaction has been created among persons of commonwealth origin because they have not been granted the same privilege of bringing their relatives to Canada as has been granted to persons of European origin living in Canada. I think that is a matter that should be carefully considered by the department and by the house.
After all the world is undergoing very great changes and I think that one of the vital matters that we have to consider within the commonwealth is the great value of the association of Pakistan, India and Ceylon with our commonwealth countries. As long as we continue to exercise any discrimination against persons of origins within other commonwealth countries so long shall we be endangering that association.
Now I know that the people of those countries, and particularly of India, realize that there are difficulties in opening wide the gates of immigration into this country, and consequently there is an arrangement between India and Canada regarding a quota system as applied to our fellow commonwealth citizens from India. I do not think that there is a quota imposed by India against Canadians who wish to reside in India. I am not sure of that but I think I am right in saying it.
On the occasion to which I refer I said:
We are now associated with a great people differ-'ing in creed, in colour and in all that guides the long evolution of a race and determines its characteristics. I hope that this will enable us in our country, and those in the countries associated with us, to end forever every vestige of racial and religious discrimination and intolerance among the people of this commonwealth.
I feel that has not been carried out and that the vestiges remain through the fact that our fellow citizens of commonwealth origin are denied the privilege of bringing their relatives to Canada, as do their fellow citizens of European origins. That is a matter of great concern to all of us and particularly, of course, to the proud people of India who have set up their independent republic but have remained associated with us in the commonwealth.
The restriction is imposed by order in council P.C. 2743 under the authority, of course, of the Immigration Act, which provides:
the provisions hereinbefore set out shall not apply to immigrants of any Asiatic race.
I am not going into that generally this morning though I hold the view that this discrimination is dangerous and also that P.C. 2115 is dangerous. We are living in a world today when we are on trial as democratic countries and our opponents in their propaganda use every possible means to show that
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration we are giving lip service to freedom, equality and democracy but that we are not fulfilling our obligations in those respects within the borders of our own country.
I want to say to the minister, apart altogether from the reference to Asiatic persons and persons of Asiatic origin in general, that particular consideration should be given to this matter of restricting the entry into Canada of relatives of those who are already happily and usefully settled in our country.
I do not want to discuss the two points involved this morning but what I want to do is focus the attention of the minister and the house on this one disability, the disability imposed upon residents of Canada, of India and commonwealth	origin-a	disability
imposed so that they may not bring into the country their close relatives except under a quota system not imposed on those of European origin. That is the point I want to bring home to the minister and I ask for reconsideration in order to remove the dissatisfaction that is quite properly felt by our compatriots of Indian origin.

I would like to follow up what has been said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I want to say at the outset that I believe the minister is doing a good job. He has begun to get hold of this whole department and is doing in my judgment an excellent job.
I am not in favour of an open-door policy at all. I believe a wisely selective and executed policy is best for our country; but at the same time I do believe that since these Indian people have come to Canada and have been granted citizenship and are proving themselves to be good citizens, and also since they have become partners in the commonwealth and are associated with the other parts of the commonwealth on a satisfactory basis, there remains no good reason why the restrictions and provisos of P.C. 2743 should continue to apply to them. I believe that the East Indian Canadian citizens should be allowed to bring their relatives on the same basis as members of any other racial group who come to Canada under the quota.
I agree with the minister that a quota should be continued on some negotiated basis, whatever it may be. Certainly I believe we should give very careful consideration indeed to placing-
Would you include relatives and friends in the quota?

Yes. As a matter of fact, I think wherever the quota is applied the East Indian people already here should be allowed to name the greater part of those who do come. I believe that would solve the situation. I think they would be happy under that sort
4262	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of agreement. There should be some sort of quota, but the major portion of those who come in the future ought to be nominated by the people who are already here.
I hope the minister will remove this restriction against the East Indian people. I do not consider for one moment that the East Indian people should be lumped in with the Asiatic races as they are now under the immigration law.

Lest there be any misunderstanding of this point I should like to say a word about it. I do not want to take any time, and I appreciate what hon. members have said. I think they may be overlooking what the practice is. In that connection, may I point out that it was the present government that negotiated the agreement with these countries which set the quota over and above that which existed up to the end of 1950. At that time a very limited number in the close relative classes could be admitted from India. In the settlement of the arrangement that 150 additional might come from that country, certain additional agreements were made. Those agreements were that preference would be given to what may be termed close relatives, though not as close as I think the hon. member would lead us to believe. Under P.C. 2115 the wife and unmarried children under certain conditions may come into the country. Then when he speaks of close relatives he may be thinking perhaps of grandchildren, brothers and sisters.
Now those persons obtain preference in the 150 quota, and to be precise we set aside I think it was 50 of the 150 for that group. To go further, I might say there were not 50 applicants, so anybody in Canada of East Indian origin who has applied for a close relative in the group the hon. members have been mentioning, and who has had his application refused, has been refused on some ground other than the quota. There was more than ample room for. all the close relatives group that have been mentioned.

I appreciate that, but is it not true that the proviso to P.C. 2743 states that the provision hereinbefore set out shall not apply to immigrants of any Asiatic race, and that that still applies to the East Indian people? What I would suggest is that whatever may be the arrangement with respect to quota, it would be advisable to remove the people of East Indian origin from the terms of the restrictive order in council.
I may say that P.C. 2743 was repealed two years ago. The hon. member is probably referring to P.Q. 2856.

I want to add my comment on this subject. I have deferred my comments because I intended to include them in the general remarks I propose to make later. Since this matter has been raised, I wish to emphasize that I do not think it is satisfactory that any arrangement for immigration into Canada for residents of India, Pakistan or Ceylon should simply be bulked in any order in council that applies to immigration from Asia.
The member for Rosetown-Biggar has pointed out that at the time we welcomed the new association with India, Pakistan and Ceylon which was established some little time ago, I expressed my pleasure that this step had been taken. At that time I indicated my own belief that by every means within our power we should demonstrate our desire to show that we recognize this partnership and regard India, Pakistan and Ceylon as belonging to a great world partnership. Anything less than that would be inclined to impair what may easily be one of the most important international relationships that now exist. I do not want to repeat the arguments I have made over and over again that there can be few things more important today than seeking to strengthen the bonds of friendship between the free nations of the British commonwealth.
There can be few experiments with greater influence on the future than the joining in a friendly arrangement of this kind of the great free nations of Asia with the nations of North America and Europe. When we hear the figures mentioned, it seems that they are strangely small in comparison with the tremendous populations of these great countries. It seems that they are inconsistent with our desire to express that friendship in practical terms. Nevertheless, those are details that could be worked out. I do urge that in whatever we do we bear in mind that any gesture which demonstrates our desire to recognize our association with India, Pakistan and Ceylon as a real, permanent partnership of free nations within the commonwealth, can be of immense advantage to the whole world.
I simply close my remarks in relation to this particular point by saying I should like the government to consider the importance and advantage of having any arrangements with those three nations of the commonwealth embraced in a separate order in council and a separate agreement. Under no circumstances should they simply be bulked with the general population of Asia, as they have been in the past.

That is precisely the point we are all trying to make to the minister. As

a matter of fact, some commonwealth countries are subject to certain regulations regarding immigration. I think these still stand. The classes of persons admissible under the order in council are, first, the husband or wife, the son, daughter, brother or sister, together with husband or wife or unmarried child; father or mother; the orphaned nephew or niece under 21 years of age of any person legally resident in Canada who is in a position to receive and care for such relative. The term "orphaned" in this connection means a person bereaved of both parents. Another class of person is a woman intending to get married, so long as the man is able to maintain his intended wife.
Where the discrimination comes in is that that seems applicable to all the commonwealth countries. We are all free and equal for purposes of immigration, and we are grouped together as persons born in or naturalized within commonwealth countries; but under another order in council, P.C. 2115, we prohibit the entry of those of any Asiatic race, except of course under the agreement that has been referred to. There is the discrimination which is irksome, and I think is understandably disliked by our fellow citizens in India and the east.

May I add to
what has been said by pointing out that the agreement with this country specifically excludes P.C. 2115. It sets out an agreement for migration from that country. That has removed the discrimination my hon. friend has spoken about.
Only to a limited extent.
Perhaps so.

I should like to ask the minister to give consideration to some temporary officers in his department who have been in the service for many years and who are still temporary. I have in my constituency a few of these men who have been working in the immigration department for probably five or six years. They own their homes and have been doing a good job. They still do not know what is going to happen; they seem to be uneasy about the future. They have approached me a couple of times. I should like to place this request before the minister and ask him if he would consider increasing the number of permanent employees in his department by a reasonable number. I think there are now some 60 or 65 permanent. I would suggest that he might bring the figure up to 75, in cases where the trend in the port is on the increase and the officers in question are perfectly satisfactory to the department.

The other question I should like to ask is with regard to the combined work of immigration and customs. In some ports apparently it has not proved to be as satisfactory as had been expected. Does the minister think that work will be carried on in the future, or have there been any changes? In some instances commercial officials have been attended by some of the immigration inspectors and some by customs and immigration inspectors. This procedure has not proven to be fully satisfactory, and I was wondering whether the minister would give us an idea as to how this procedure has worked out in the last year or so.

Thank you.
Is the minister going to make a general statement on immigration policy? I had hoped to catch the chairman's eye earlier but I am raising the question now.
I had one ready, Mr. Chairman, but the hon. member for Middlesex East intervened first in the debate and we have been proceeding from that point.
Will the minister make the statement now?

I think so.
Mr. Chairman, in presenting the annual report on immigration I should like to deal with the many things which occurred before and during the year 1951 which gave rise to the largest and most successful immigrant year since the war. Before doing so, however, it would be just as well for me to re-state the policy of immigration to which I have referred on every occasion that I have presented a report to the house. That policy is to admit to Canada in numbers not exceeding the absorptive capacity of our country and without altering the fundamental character of our people, such persons as are likely to contribute to our national life.
This department was created in January 1950, though, of course, it was a combination of branches of government already at that time functioning. When the first estimates were presented in this house, many members said that the government was not doing much about immigration, that we had no plan for immigration; that they were quite dissatisfied with the reduction in the number of immigrants from 1948, when there were 125,000 admitted, to 1949 when there were about

90,000	admitted. During the debates in the spring of 1950, while no figure was placed upon the numbers who might come in, many stated that 90,000 was not sufficient. I think this was in keeping with the opinion of nearly all members of the house who spoke in the debates, at the end of the war, about immigration. There had been almost unanimous approval for the admission to Canada of people from Europe, especially those persons who had a claim upon our charity by reason of the unfortunate plight in which they found themselves. In addition, everyone recognized that Canada could only grow substantially if it grew by taking immigrants as well as by natural growth. And it was generally agreed that Canada should grow in numbers so as to be able to develop our great resources. The debates of 1945-6-7-8 show clearly that parliament was almost unanimous in its belief that immigration as a policy was desirable. Believing as we did that immigration could assist in the building of our country and people, we undertook throughout 1950 every step which we thought was in the interests of the Canadian people to stimulate immigration, without at the same time imposing upon the Canadian taxpayer any expense which was not justified.

As we saw it in the fall and winter of
1950-51, there was an unsatisfied demand for almost every form of labour in Canada. As well there was a demand for farm settlers because of the regularly changing population on the farm. In addition, there were complaints that the re-armament program was not progressing fast enough. So it became known abroad that Canada was accepting immigrants and large numbers made arrangements to come to what they were sure was the country of the future.
I am satisfied that everything which could have been done last year to stimulate immigration was done; and I am satisfied, sir, that those who came here were not only welcome, they were actually needed.
May I have consent to table a statement for the calendar year 1951 as well as the five months' statement for this year that I mentioned earlier?

When the supplementary estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration were being considered I gave the house certain undertakings that at the appropriate time I would deal with certain matters.

We hear, of course, about the man who does not live up to his obligations. We hear nothing much about the thousands who do and the result has been that the small percentage of defaulting farm workers stand out in unfortunate contrast to the others.
One of the objects of the Canadian immigration policy is to build up Canadian agriculture. We are doing that and in proof of that statement I would put on the record the achievement of just one racial group, those from the Netherlands. It is true those from the Netherlands are, perhaps, a little different from the average farm labourer. Their roots are perhaps a little more deeply in the soil. They move as a family unit in many cases and the selection is made with the co-operation of Netherlands authorities.
However, from the inception of the movement from Holland, up until March 30, 1952, a total of about fifteen thousand Dutch families had come forward to Canada. Of

these more than 4,500 families are now farming on their own account, either as farm owners or farm tenants. Many thousands more are still employed on the farms of Canadians, learning Canadian methods, saving their money and planning for the time when they will have farms of their own.
It would, of course, be possible to take steps which would ensure that the man who says he is coming to Canada as a farm worker remains a farm worker. We could even hold the possibility of deportation over his head, as indeed is done in some countries. However, it is my opinion that the Canadian people would be entirely opposed to any such practice. It would be contrary to the whole Canadian belief in freedom of the individual.
It is much better, I believe, to ensure through our selection that the farm labourer who comes to Canada comes from a farming background in his homeland, and is of a type most likely to make a lifetime career out of farming in Canada.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was anxious to know whether in our planning we took into account the jobs available and the areas in which they were available, and whether consideration was given to the countries from which immigrants are selected. The answer in both cases is "yes". First of all I want to make it clear that no policy of immigration can be operated on a stop and go basis. We cannot possibly develop that policy on a plan that calls for one specific immigrant for one specific opportunity. We must be prepared to have faith in our country and the opportunity it will offer to those prepared to work. This means that if we believe in Canada's future, if we believe ours is a developing country, we must be prepared to bring in some people, knowing that when they are on the ground Canada will have a place for them.
In regard to the question of planning and the countries of selection, I wish to assure the house that every effort is being made to increase the number of immigrants from the United Kingdom and France, and I am glad to report that during the fiscal year
1951-52 a total of 36,000 immigrants of English, Scottish, Irish and Welsh origin came to Canada, as compared with 15,429 in the previous fiscal year. From France we received 6,666 as compared with 1,845. We also had a large intake of people from the northern European countries which in the past have contributed a good type of immigrant, who have readily become integrated into the
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Canadian communities in which they have made their homes. I . think every debate on immigration has indicated that it is the desire of this house that we should have a substantial number from northern Europe.
Earlier in the session there were some questions about the assisted passage scheme. The assisted passage plan was suspended last October but has again been in operation since the supplementary estimates were passed.
Under this plan the government advanced to the immigrant a substantial portion of his fare to Canada, provided that he was entering an occupation in Canada where there was definite need of his services. The advance is considered a loan and is recoverable in monthly instalments over a maximum period of two years.
As at the end of May a total of 16,255 had come to Canada under the assisted passage plan, and $2,746,006 had been advanced in fares. So far the record of repayment has been good, and it is anticipated that by the end of July a total in excess of $1 million will have been repaid.
There are two other matters on which I promised information to the house. The first of these concerns those whose establishment in Canada is delayed through no fault of their own, who become indigent as a result of sickness or accident. We have been in communication with all provincial governments in regard to these people and have offered to assume, under some circumstances, half the costs of hospitalization and welfare expended on their behalf. An agreement to this effect has been signed with the province of Ontario and negotiations are continuing with the other nine provinces. I should like to table a copy of that agreement.
The other matter concerns the issuing of fraudulent visas. Earlier in the session I gave the house all the information I felt I could give at the time in view of the investigation which was then going on. I am still somewhat limited in the information I can provide on this matter, but I can report that the investigation by officers of the R.C.M.P. has now been virtually completed. Agents of the Department of Justice have before them the report of the R.C.M.P. and in addition a total of more than 1,200 exhibits which are being carefully studied.
I believe I have completed my undertakings which I gave to hon. members, but I should like to say a word about the quality of the immigrants coming to Canada. A few weeks ago in this house a return was made which indicated that in the past two years a total of 193 new industries had been established in Canada through investment of foreign
4270	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration capital. Not all these were immigrant industries, of course, but a significant percentage of them were.
It is true that in the years immediately following world war II a substantial percentage of our immigrants were displaced persons, but that percentage has been decreasing and more and more of those coming to Canada have come from a background of employment and the home. Last year only 22 per cent were in the displaced person category. The remainder were people who came to Canada voluntarily because they saw here a developing country, a country with an expanding economy which offered opportunity to those who would work. These people do not arrive here penniless. True, the money they can bring is restricted by currency regulations, but in the calendar year 1951 they brought to Canada more than $60 million in new capital. They brought in other capital, but they also brought skills and all of them and their dependents were consumers from the moment of their arrival here. That, I suggest, is an important aspect of immigration.
Indications for 1952 are that the intake may not reach the 1951 figure. Because of the improved situation in regard to shipping we have been able to move to Canada in the first five months of the year a total of 82,000 persons, but it is expected as well that the figures will decline beginning this month, and it is not the intention of the government to admit certain workers after the end of October.
Substantially higher are the figures for British immigration which totalled 18,665 for the	first five months of	this year
as compared with 10,599 for the first five months of 1951, and indeed a figure which exceeds our total British immigration in the calendar year 1950 by over
5,000.	The figures from France are also up, with 2,426 arriving in the first five months of 1952 as compared with 1,747 in the same five months a year ago. The figures for other countries, while greater, are not so in proportion. It would appear that this year there will be a greater percentage from the United Kingdom and northern Europe and a smaller percentage from the other countries. For example, for the first five months 23 per cent of all immigrants were from the United Kingdom as compared with 17J per cent in 1951; 38 per cent were from northern Europe as compared with 34 per cent in 1951; and 39 per cent were from other countries as compared with 48i per cent in 1951.
I should like to place on Hansard for the benefit of all hon. members a summary of those persons who are admissible to Canada, made up according to the countries of origin

and indicating the occupations, the close relative groups and the like, so that hon. members may know precisely who is admissible from what particular country. This statement indicates that they shall not be so dealt with in the future.

speechtext:
I wish to devote a very few minutes to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Substantially I want to compliment the minister on what I think has been a very excellent job done for the Canadian people. Oh, there have been complaints. I remember in Vancouver last winter when for a very short time we had 200 or 300 people who had to be accommodated in an immigration shed, and there were complaints from labour and from other people too that we were bringing people here who could not be accommodated. I hope we will balance this off against the very substantial and infinitely greater number of cases of people who have come to this country in the last two or three years, have become admirably established and have made a great contribution to Canada in their new skills, their new outlook and their old background, if I may say so.
There has been a great deal of success. We hear very little of the success. We hear a great deal of the odd failure. I want to suggest to the minister, in line with the remark of the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth, that we should probably pay a little more attention in a practical way to settling farm
4, 1952	4271
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration immigrants. I think the majority of those people, coming from the northern part of Europe and being independent people, would prefer to work on their own farms as soon as they possibly could after coming here instead of working for someone else.
I have the idea that is a field in which the federal administration could work with the provinces by way of modest loans in setting up farm population on some of our newer land. In the northern half of British Columbia we have vast areas of splendid land which could be opened up, but in many instances these people are coming over with inadequate sums of money.
There are those who say people are not coming in fast enough, that we need people quickly and so on, but we should bear in mind that many countries in Europe are not anxious to lose their people and have set up regulations pertaining to the export of money and so on as a bar to their leaving.
I think in the main we have done a good job. I want to compliment the minister upon his action with regard to one or two minority groups which by and large we have looked upon in the past if not as being undesirable, at least as being difficult to work into the fabric of Canadian life. I refer first to the Chinese who came to Canada in the early part of the century in great numbers. Then we adopted a closed door policy against them. In recent years the minister and his department has given attention to bringing over some of the close relatives of these people.
I want to say a word on behalf of another group of people who are part of the brotherhood within the commonwealth of nations, the East Indians. We have at the present time in British Columbia approximately 2,000 East Indians. I remember distinctly in 1913 when a boat arrived in Vancouver with a great number of East Indians aboard who were seeking entry into Canada. Entry was refused and the ship remained in harbour for many weeks, and finally had to return these people to India. Out of that incident arose a disruption of relations between peoples who were together at that time under the British crown, and it did not do us any good across the years.
The recent proposal announced by the minister is to bring in 150 East Indians a year. This is a small number, but it will do something to help cure an old sore. We are finding now, both in the case of the East Indians and the Chinese, that these people have become well educated. Our East Indians have improved their lot in British Columbia, where many of them are now mill owners. I have in mind one who is No. 2 air pilot for
4272	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the Canadian Pacific Air Lines and is going to fly the Pacific when they inaugurate their schedule.
I want to compliment whoever may have been responsible-probably it was the civil service-for the appointment of an East Indian to the bureau of statistics here in Ottawa. This man is a graduate of the University of British Columbia and is admirably versed in mathematics. We should bear in mind that although Canada is small in population, it is rapidly achieving a foremost position among the nations of the world because of our resources and the integrity of the people. A spirit of open-mindedness with regard to immigration from various countries of the world will do much to add to our stature, but we should bring in only the best people. Again I repeat that the minister has done an admirable job for us in this matter of immigration to our country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word or two. The minister's statement certainly added something to the situation, but I must confess that the chief impression I got was that there was an agreement under which Canada would admit a certain number of people in each group. The minister indicated that there was a general feeling in favour of greater immigration, but I got only the most general Impression as to any policy which is to be followed or any set of principles which is to be adopted. However, I am not going to plunge into that further at this time.
I have in mind a few questions I should like to ask on administration matters. One feels that there is overlapping between the Department of Labour and the department of immigration. Inevitably some of those who are admitted eventually become public charges, and the best information I can get indicates that there is overlapping there. Those in need are able to get help from both labour and immigration; sometimes they are able to get it also from welfare groups, ethnic societies and individual sponsors. I do not think the minister will disagree with me when I say that from one point of view there is what you might call a partnership between the departments, but from another point of view there is overlapping.
Then another question comes to my mind. In this assisted passage scheme I understand the assistance is given to the worker but not to his wife and children. That leaves him with a tremendous task on his hands when he arrives here, because he has to pay back his own passage, support his family while they are in Europe, and get the money to bring them out. These are some of the questions in my mind, and perhaps the minister would deal with them and one or two others that I should like to ask later.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA SHOWING SEX, OCCUPATION AND DESTINATION FOR THE FIVE MONTHS ENDED MAY 31, 1952
speechtext:
I suppose it would be true to say that there is overlapping in the sense that the Department of Labour and the department of immigration, both abroad and here, interest themselves in the immigrant. However, it has been found by experience since the war that there are

separate functions for each department, both tending to aid the immigrant in becoming settled in Canada. For example, before this department as such was set up the Department of Labour administered the movement of people under IRO. They continued to do that until the end of last year, when IRO ceased to function. To that extent it might have been desirable that there should be a division of responsibility. The purpose of the overlapping both here and abroad is very simple. We desire to have the best possible information as to opportunities in Canada, and in addition we want to have the best possible judgment as to the suitability of the applicants abroad. Labour can be of assistance in that regard.
When the immigrant comes to this country he may be placed by labour if he happens to be one of these refugees under IRO; and if he happens to be placed by immigration and in due course finds himself out of employment, naturally he is entitled to the assistance of the national employment service, and of the placement service of our own department. So far as I am concerned, I am satisfied that the two departments each contribute something to the choice of the immigrant and to the settlement of the immigrant in this country.
With respect to the assisted passage scheme, I agree that we do not extend it to the dependents of a worker; and that is a debatable point. It may not be desirable on social grounds to separate the head of the family from the dependents for any length of time, and an argument can be made that if we advance money to bring forward the head of the family we could also advance money for the dependents. That of course would not apply in the case of a single immigrant. The purpose of the assisted passage scheme originally was to provide the means of bringing to Canada some person who was needed here, having in mind as well that the chances would be that he could probably make a go of it and find the means of bringing forward his family.
I agree if the family is large and if the immigrant happens to go to British Columbia, it will cost a great deal of money to bring his wife and children forward. That is one of the weaknesses of the assisted passage scheme but I think it is one of the weaknesses that must be accepted with the desire to bring the person in the first place.

In the first instance I should ike to thank the minister for answering the question I asked him on March 28 with regard :o the policy of the department. His state-nent was not quite as comprehensive as I roped it would be, but he has assisted in our
4, 1952	4273
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration understanding of the problem. I think the subject of immigration requires greater understanding on the part of the Canadian people. I believe there is a wide diversity of opinion with regard to the benefits or otherwise of immigration. We tend to look back to the period of the early years of this century when immigrants came into our country in very large numbers and were largely bent on taking up farm lands, particularly in western Canada. We consider there was considerable success attached to that great movement of people. At the present time it is not possible to absorb people into Canada on that scale and with that intention, as it was in those earlier years. The subject of immigration has become somewhat more complicated and deserves very careful attention.
With the growing industrialization of our country and the trend toward urbanization there is no question but that the immigrant is not as easily placed as he was in the first twenty years of this century. That is why I have been wondering about our immigration policy. Let me put this question to the minister. Over a period of years what increase in the population of Canada can be attributed to immigration? Has the minister at his disposal information that will indicate to us the relationship between immigration, natural increase and loss of population to the United States and other countries? Would we be further ahead in putting more emphasis on attempting to retain the natural increase of our country rather than putting our efforts into drawing immigrants into Canada? There is no question but that there is a serious loss of people each year to the United States and elsewhere.
It is on these grounds that I say there is perhaps a lack of understanding throughout Canada as to immigration. Is it as valuable as we have sometimes thought it to be? I do not suggest for one minute that we have not received immense contributions from immigrant people. After all, we ourselves are either immigrants or the descendants of immigrants, and the country has benefited from those who have come here in the past and from those who are coming at the present time. But is our emphasis perhaps wrongly placed? I should like to have the minister's comments on that problem. One of the reasons I raise it is that checking in the Canada Year Book for 1951 I noticed according to paragraph 13 on page 152, which deals with presumed permanent movement of population between Canada and the United States for the years ending June 30, 1940 to 1949, that over that period we
4274	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration appear to have lost to the United States 131,742 persons. That is our net loss to that country.
The figures there appear to indicate that not only do our native born depart to the United States but also many people who have not established themselves as permanent residents, immigrants who have entered our country just as a stopping place before going elsewhere. When we are spending several millions of dollars on immigration, are we aware of the fact that we are losing many of our immigrants and perhaps many of our native born who, with a somewhat different emphasis with respect to our economy, might be retained within the country?
I have a number of problems I should like to take up with the minister. I do not propose to use too much of the time of the house, but I think this department requires careful study for our own information and for the information of the people of Canada. I should like to draw the minister's attention to an article which I presume he has already seen, and perhaps has answered, though I did not see the answer in the press. This article is dated April 26, 1952, and appeared in the Globe and Mail. It has reference to a meeting of the school of social work of the University of Toronto and the Toronto welfare council. The subject dealt with was immigration. From my knowledge of the situation in Winnipeg, and from my experience with the Winnipeg welfare council, I vrould say that the problems discussed in this article are perhaps the same in western Canada as they are in Ontario. I would like to quote just one or two passages here and perhaps the minister will make some comment. The article starts off as follows:
Prospective newcomers should be given a start in basic English before they arrive in Canada and the process of integrating them into the Canadian way of life needs a major overhauling.
These were two of the views expressed last night at a conference on new immigrants, held under the auspices of the school of social work of the University of Toronto, and the Toronto welfare council.
Then further on: Professor C. D. Hendry, who is director of the social work school, dealt with the problems facing the services. This is the statement made by Professor Hendry:
The public as a whole, he said, seemed to lack clarity, conviction and certainty as to how many immigrants can be absorbed. He described public policy on immigration as: "Cautious, conservative but essentially constructive." Dealing with specific attitudes, he found unawareness, lack of information, and apathy prevailed in some quarters, while in others there was fear that job security of Canadians was threatened by the immigrants.


He goes on to say, and these are his exact words as given in quotation marks in the paper; speaking of agency officials-
"I regret to say some are cold and even harsh in their treatment of new citizens."
Dr. Hendry has some further comments along that line and then Professor Wolfgang Friedmann, of the school of law, University of Toronto, and again I am quoting from the newspaper, said:
Many things could be done before the immigrants arrive in Canada. A common bond united all agencies which dealt with one or another of the problems of immigrants; a common desire to meet the challenge offered by the arrival in Canada of 200,000 newcomers annually.
Then Stephen Davidovitch, adviser, citizenship branch, Ontario department of education, said:
-the lot of the present-day immigrant was infinitely better than that of the immigrant of 50 years ago. Generally speaking, the public agreed that the immigrant should be helped but not mollycoddled.
I think we are in agreement with that.
An association composed of representatives of ethnic groups, to meet the immigrant and advise him on such matters as housing and jobs, would be a distinct advancement, he felt. Such a body might also make loans to newcomers and in this way prevent them from being fleeced by tricksters. . . Education of the newcomer, particularly in English, was stressed by the speaker as a prime necessity.
Miss Florence Philpott, executive secretary, Toronto welfare council, said:
A great deal of commendable work had been done. She stressed the lack of integrated, co-ordinated program.
After reviewing the existing services available to immigrants, Miss Philpott remarked that far too few of them availed themselves of their use. The fact that many of the agencies had not informed the immigrants of the existence of these services was not surprising, Miss Philpott said. She doubted whether these agencies knew the services existed, either.
What I am wondering about, Mr. Chairman, is the amount of co-operation that exists between this department and the various provincial governments on whom apparently the final responsibility rests when the immigrants are admitted. In experience, a great deal of the work in connection with immigrants seems to fall upon voluntary organizations and welfare services. To what extent the department has a plan with regard to aiding immigrants on arrival, in conjunction with the province, as suggested in that article, is a question on which I would like to hear some comment from the minister.
I will stop at that point, though I have some other questions to take up later.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA SHOWING SEX, OCCUPATION AND DESTINATION FOR THE FIVE MONTHS ENDED MAY 31, 1952
speechtext:
Before we pass this item, I want to suggest that perhaps what is happening this afternoon indicates the advantage to any important department of holding its estimates off until the last moment. This subject is being discussed in an atmosphere of complacency that is wholly out of line with the sentiments of the people of this country generally toward the administration of this department. It has already been said today, and I feel sure it is true, that next to the burden of taxation and the high cost of living there is no single subject about which there is as much dissatisfaction as there is in regard to our over-all policy of immigration.
But there is one subject to which I wish to refer before this passes from discussion in this house into the wider discussion that undoubtedly will be carried on in the press and in public, as it has been so vigorously for some months. I refer to the implications of the disclosure of corruption and fraud amongst various officials attached to this department. I refer once again to an article that has been referred to before, the article in Maclean's magazine of March 15 of this year under the title, "How racketeers sold entry into Canada.'' I would also refer to an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of February 21 of this year under the heading "Immigration by fraud," referring to disclosures that there had been fraud in connection with illegal entry into Canada of an undisclosed number of persons through the activities of an
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

agent of this department at Karlsruhe, Germany. The article in Maclean's magazine of March 15 referred to the activities of government officials in connection with immigration from Italy. The statements were unequivocal; they were positive. This article by one of the best known writers in this country contains this positive statement at the top:
Corrupt Canadian government officials and unscrupulous travel agencies have extorted thousands of dollars to smuggle Italian immigrants into Canada.
The minister has simply referred to this by indicating that an inquiry has advanced to the stage where it may be hoped that it can be closed at an early date. I suggest that this indicates something of a nature that calls for the most thoroughgoing investigation, and not merely an investigation of a possible breach of trust or criminal action. The Maclean's article on the one hand, and the Ottawa Journal editorial on the other, I merely choose as examples of the many editorials and public statements that have been made indicating widespread concern about something that may by no manner of means be confined to the known cases which have been indicated in this way. It is not usual that it is only the known cases that emerge in the way these did before there were any investigations, so far as we are aware.
In connnection with the Maclean's article to which I have referred, it speaks of a widespread organization, describes the methods by which an agency named in this article had been carrying on activities; and it describes how a man, named, obtained false declarations that certain people were getting certain farmers to work for them. This article also refers to the information which had been obtained that similar activities had been carried on in Germany.
There are two angles to a disclosure of this kind. The first is the breach of trust by the officials. The second is the fact that if these people, as citizens of Canada, were obtaining money by false pretences and had broken their trust, then criminal prosecutions should follow. Third, and extremely important, there is the situation that is produced by the activities of these people in connection with immigration itself. On the one hand there would appear to have been a substantial entry into Canada of immigrants who should not have come. On the other hand it would appear that many immigrants who could have come in any event were paying sums of money to these officials in the mistaken idea that this was necessary in order to enter Canada.
It is not just enough to be told what action has been taken in relation to the officials.

It is also necessary to know what is going to be done with regard to the immigrants. As to these immigrants who paid money unnecessarily to these men who have broken their trust and are probably also guilty of criminal offences, certainly if it is humanly possible that money should be obtained, and paid back to the immigrants. It may not be possible. Most certainly it is an unfortunate thing if their innocent paying of this money means that there is no way by which they can recover.
But the other side of this picture is that those who have obtained entry into Canada by fraud may well have come here for purposes of which we are only too well aware at this time. Therefore any conduct of this nature, in breaking the immigration laws of Canada at such a time as this, should be looked upon with particular concern. I would hope that the investigations that are taking place will be completed soon; that prompt action will be taken to deal with every single case disclosed; that a complete and comprehensive public statement will be made with regard to every aspect of this situation as disclosed in part by the earlier information which was made public in the manner I have described, so the real concern in the minds of the people of Canada may be allayed at least in some measure and there may be an assurance that the laxity which permitted fraud of this nature will be checked so that in future the immigration laws and such immigration policy as may exist will in fact be enforced by the officials of the department.
Just before I close these remarks may I say that no remark I have made is to be taken as a reflection on the regular officials of the department here who, I know, give that kind of service one would expect. But here are disclosures of fraud on the part of people who in some way were permitted to have an influence upon the entry into Canada of immigrants, and it is a situation which calls for action of a nature which will reassure the public with regard to the procedure that is being followed.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA SHOWING SEX, OCCUPATION AND DESTINATION FOR THE FIVE MONTHS ENDED MAY 31, 1952
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I assure the leader of the opposition that when the information came to the ears of this department that there were any irregularities at all, we began the investigation some time before any publicity appeared about it. In fact it was the action taken by this department in connection with certain legal matters which drew it to the attention of the public.
There are several problems involved, as he has said. First, what action is to be taken with respect to the immigration officer 55704-2701
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration who permitted himself to be found breaking his trust? Second, what is to be done with respect to that person who induced him to do so? Third, what is to be done with respect to others who knowingly, and perhaps not knowingly, contributed to the activities of this group?
I must say that I personally have been disappointed at the progress which has been made in going through the many matters involved. When I say I was disappointed, I mean that I was disappointed only in the length of time it has taken, but not in the work that has been done. When I discussed this matter as late as Tuesday night of this week with some of the officials of the Department of Justice, I fully appreciated the time that was required to go thoroughly into the whole question as it may affect all the persons concerned in Canada and abroad. Just as soon as we have come to a conclusion as to the extent of the activity and the means to take to bring before the courts those who have broken our laws, we shall do so; and at the same time, within the rules which apply when matters are before the courts, we shall give as much information as possible to the public.
I want to thank the leader of the opposition for his reference to the officials of the department. I knew he would say what he has said when he remembered that he had not done so previously. I think the use of the headline in the one article was misleading, as I pointed out to the hon. member for Kamloops at one time this session. It is commonly understood that the term "officials", when related to the civil service, means a particular group of people. I want to assure the committee that no official I know of is concerned in this matter.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA SHOWING SEX, OCCUPATION AND DESTINATION FOR THE FIVE MONTHS ENDED MAY 31, 1952
speechtext:
There is one point I wish to refer to briefly; I am speaking particularly of education for adult immigrants. There can be no doubt about the ordinary educational facilities being available to those of the ordinary education age. It is extremely important that adult immigrants have an opportunity for education which not only gives them the advantage of the two official languages of Canada but also gives them information with regard to our form of democracy and with regard to many things about our country which are of importance. The textbooks that are being supplied by the department in that respect are very good and are being used to great advantage.
I believe more could be done through an extension of the co-operation between the department and the departments of education of the provinces than is being done at the moment. On this occasion I am not raising this critically, because we are dealing with a relatively new field. I simply put this forward and leave the thought as something I should like to have considered by the department.
More and more we recognize the advantage of visual instruction. I would hope that a conference between some representative or representatives of the department and representatives of departments of education in the provinces would consider the possibility of arranging for a type of visual education which could be produced by the national film board and would become generally available across the country. Certain films are available now, but these films are not of the type I have in mind. Films which illustrate in a pictorial form certain types of our system of national, provincial and .educational government, certain types of our


own characteristic Canadian way of doing things in different parts of the country, would all be very helpful in connection with these programs.
In offering this suggestion may I pay my personal tribute to some of these voluntary organizations which, along with the organizations set up by the provincial governments, are doing a magnificent job at this time in giving educational training to the immigrants. I do not propose to pick them out, because in some cases they are religious organizations, in some cases they are under particular racial groups, and under various public service activities. But a splendid job is being done which deserves the commendation of hon. members and the people of Canada. I am only suggesting that with the experience already behind us, it would be desirable that we extend the facilities for visual education and assist education in every way we can through the opportunities we now have.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA SHOWING SEX, OCCUPATION AND DESTINATION FOR THE FIVE MONTHS ENDED MAY 31, 1952
speechtext:
I agree that one of the best means of education is the visual method and, as the leader of the opposition has indicated, we have films; but at one time or another there has been some criticism, not criticism of the films we have but merely, as my hon. friend has said, a request for other and perhaps better films. I want to assure him that in the citizenship branch we are doing what we can to provide these, and we shall take under advisement the recommendation he has made.
I do want to join with him in again expressing my thanks to all the organizations which contribute to this work. I have said repeatedly that we could not function in providing the immigrant with an easy means of entry into Canadian life without them. In fact I have gone farther and said that if they did not do it I do not know who would, unless the government did it. But I think it is recognized that it is not desirable that we should provide all the means, because those means are provided by voluntary organizations on the spot, by zealous workers who know local circumstances and who, because of their interest in these people and their interest in the Canadian people as a whole, have volunteered their help. It is a most remarkable work, and I think it is having most remarkable results.

I want to refer briefly to a subject already discussed, not for the purpose of reopening it but simply to indicate that I support the proposal which was placed before the minister. Unfortunately another engagement prevented me from being here when the matter was first raised. I refer to the question of allowing Canadians of East Indian origin to bring into the country their

relatives from India. The proposal, which has been set forth in detail in a brief submitted by the Khalsa Diwan society of Vancouver, is that the Indian people be treated for this purpose not along with the general classification of persons of Asiatic race, but that they be regarded as what in fact they are, members of the commonwealth, so the restriction applicable at the present time under the provisions of P.C. 2743 would not apply with respect to Canadian citizens of East Indian origin who are anxious to bring their relatives into Canada.
As I say, this matter has been discussed previously; and it is for the purpose of indicating that I too support the suggestions which have been made to the minister that I bring it up at this time. I do so particularly because I have some knowledge of the splendid contribution the East Indians are making to the social and economic life of Canada. We have a quite substantial group of them in Kamloops. They are engaged very successfully in farming, lumbering and all other types of activities which contribute in a very real way to the economic as well as the social welfare of our part of the country.
Just as a final illustration I should like to say that recently I had occasion to submit to the minister an application for the inclusion in the current quota of some relatives of one of those East Indians who lives in Kamloops. The application was supported by a group of prominent citizens who signed a letter to the effect that they supported the application. It was remarkable to see who signed that letter. There was the past mayor of Kamloops, the present mayor, the bank managers, prominent citizens in every walk of life, social and business in that city and district. I think that indicates the very high regard in which these people are held in the communities where they are settled and where they are good Canadians.
I do hope the minister and his officials will find it possible to discontinue the restrictions on the applications from those of East Indian origin who are Canadian citizens for the admission of their relatives to Canada. I regret I was not here when it was discussed, and that it is necessary to go back to the subject, but I want to make it clear that I support the recommendations made.

speechtext:
