294. To provide for the civil defence program and to authorize total commitments against future years in the amount of $575,000, $6,508,839.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this item was before the committee on June 6 and has been standing since. At that time the hon. member for Calgary East raised the point that although a larger amount is being asked for this year, $6,508,839 as compared with $4,196,202 last year, only $844,851 was spent. Certain explanations were given. In fact an attempt was made to rather chide the hon. member for raising the question by pointing out that, on the one hand, arguments were made in favour of economy and, on the other hand, when money was not spent questions were raised about that. The discussion ended at that stage.
Although we have reached this stage in the session I do not think the matter should be left in that position. We are asked to consider an appropriation of $6,508,839 for civil defence. What was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary East was that although $4,196,202 was provided last year, only $844,851 was spent. In doing that he was naturally raising the question why there should be an increased appropriation asked for this year.
The very fact that an attempt was made to divert attention from the question asked by suggesting that there was a surprising contrast in a request for economy, on the one hand, and then questions raised as to why
4280	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare the whole amount was not spent indicates the measure of unreality with which we are dealing with this subject.
Civil defence is as important as it is described from time to time by the minister or by those attached to the department, or it is not. Generally speaking there does not seem to be any measure of urgency that is in keeping with the statements that are made from time to time. We seem to be proceeding with this at a rather leisurely pace which is wholly inconsistent with the statements that are made about the seriousness of world affairs. The day before yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke in Winnipeg and, according to a Canadian Press dispatch, said:
The free world must be prepared for an Increase in tension in Europe.
The possibility of accidentally "slipping" into a third world war will increase in the next two or three months until German ratification is decided one way or another.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs was emphasizing the urgency of the situation which might develop within the next few months, yet we are told that to a substantial extent the difficulty in proceeding with civil defence is that there are no agreements with some of the provinces. So far as I have been able to ascertain agreements have been made with only two provinces, Ontario and Alberta. This covers only part of the problem.
Under these agreements payments will be made by the dominion government for part of the civil defence activities and for certain responsibilities that would arise. For instance, in the case of the agreement with Ontario there is an undertaking in connection with the extremely important question of uniformity of hose couplings so that fire equipment from one community may be used in another, which proved to be of such immense value in the United Kingdom and other countries which were bombed during the last war.
The minister who is responsible for this activity quoted a statement by Sir John Hodsoll, appearing in the Montreal Star of May 9, who had visited this country to inquire into civil defence activities, as he had in the United States. He was reported to have expressed his approval of what he found in Canada. I am not aware of how much of Canada Sir John Hodsoll saw, but it is just possible that he may have been beguiled by some of this most effective propaganda that emanates from the department of the minister who is responsible for this particular task.
Nevertheless we are not as much concerned with what may be said by somebody from outside Canada about what is happening here


as we are with what we know is actually taking place in Canada. We know that no effective civil defence organization is in existence across this country at this time. We know that if, to use the considered terms of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we should slip into another war within the next two or three months we would not be ready to deal with the problems that would arise in the case of attack.
I hope no one will suggest that I am being an alarmist when I speak in these terms. I am referring to the statement of the minister for external affairs that such a possibility exists. If it does exist, then we should be considering this subject with the sense of urgency that is related to a statement of that kind by the minister responsible for our external affairs. We should know to what extent steps have been taken or should be taken to deal with first aid, with firefighting, with the designation of target areas, with the setting up of reception areas, with mutual aid to communities, and matters of that kind. We should know to what extent these arrangements are known to those who will be responsible for carrying them out. We should also know something of what has been done in regard to the establishment of emergency hospitals, emergency transportation and engineering services. We also should know something about the organization that would integrate the activities of the dominion, provincial and municipal services that would be brought together. I am not going to go into the field of civil defence, because that is a very broad field indeed. However, one thing that is clear is that there cannot be an effective civil defence organization under the plans now contemplated until there are agreements with the provinces. The necessity for those agreements is indicated by the very fact that there are agreements now with Ontario and Alberta covering only a limited part of this problem, it is true, but still covering some part of it.
The minister has already indicated certain difficulties that will exist until these agreements are completed. Either this is something real or it is not. If it is something real, then we need an organization that can go into operation right away. If it is not real then we should not be asked to vote more than $6 million for this particular task, remembering that the $6 million is only a limited part of the over-all cost of the civil defence organization that would be set up through the activities of the dominion, provincial and municipal organizations. If this is something that is important, if there is in fact a danger and that danger should become a reality, is it going to be any answer to anybody in this country who suffers as a result to say that

we did not have an agreement with your province, we were not able to convince them that civil defence was really a provincial problem?
Civil defence and the assurance of civil ' defence surely must be a national responsibility. Surely it can be no answer, in the event that a situation should arise calling for civil defence, to say, "oh, we did not achieve any agreements". Actually some of the provincial governments, and perhaps all of them, do not believe it is their responsibility. Some of them have made a move toward entering into agreements or have entered into agreements because they feel that something must be done in any event, but surely civil defence is a part of the whole problem of defence. Surely if civil defence is necessary, whatever steps are necessary to assure civil defence should be taken. Surely this extra burden imposed because of world conditions, over which no provincial government and no municipal authority can have any control, should not be added to the already heavy burden of the provincial and municipal governments.
At a time when municipal councils are having all the difficulties they can handle it does not seem reasonable that this new burden, wholly unrelated to the ordinary municipal tasks, should toe added to what has already been thrown upon them. I suggest that no matter what may have happened before, no matter what may have been regarded as adequate under the circumstances, if the government really thinks the Secretary of State for External Affairs is correctly interpreting the situation when he predicts that the next two or three months are going to be as critical as any months that lie ahead of us, months within which, to use his words, "there is a possibility of slipping into war", we should be doing more than we are doing now to tackle this problem with a sense of urgency and reality.
I do wish to say that the officer in charge of civil defence, Major General Worthington, is an officer whose experience, energy and adaptability to new conditions command the confidence of all who know him and undoubtedly should command the confidence of all Canadians. I cannot imagine any officer in Canada who could more effectively perform that task on the basis of his record in the different military and other duties that he has undertaken. But this problem relates to a fundamental decision as to whether there is urgency and necessity for civil defence. If there is, then 1 suggest that an acceptance of the responsibility by the dominion government calls for action to meet any situation which may arise in keeping with the possibilities,
Supply-Health and Welfare remote as we hope they are, that have been pictured within the past few days by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. No one wishes to be an alarmist, but there would be no reason for the organization of civil defence at all unless it were against the possibility of just such a situation as is contemplated by the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In the light of that statement, in the light of world events related to it, and having regard to the vital importance of civil defence in the preservation of our whole economy and the confidence of our people, I feel that the problem should be tackled with a sense of reality that does not yet seem to have emerged.
Let me point out one of the things which should be in the mind of every one of us. We have heard a great deal in the past few days about the bombing of the power plants on the Yalu river. I am not going to enter into the controversy relating to that bombing.
I should imagine that most young Canadians in Korea will have very definite views as to the desirability of permitting electricity from that source to be used to assist the communists in their efforts to build up their military strength. Nevertheless I think that having regard to the importance of these targets and the extent to which it was clear that they were given a No. 1 priority, we should remember that in this country a higher percentage of industry is based upon electrical power than in any other great industrial country in the world.
In every area which would be open to an attack of that kind, part of the general morale of our people would be related to the plans which might be made in keeping with the knowledge of that simple fact. I know we have not time for an extended debate on this subject. I am putting my views forward at this time with the hope that they may be given consideration, particularly in the light of the assessment of world affairs made only two days ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said, there is not time for the kind of discussion which he and I would like to have on this important matter. I can only say that generally speaking I agree with what he has said. That does not mean to say that in all particulars as to the division of responsibility he and I would be in full accord, but generally speaking I want him to know that in a general way I agree with what he has said.
The policy we pursue is one of decentralization. That is the practice followed in the United Kingdom where they have had perhaps the greatest experience in civil

Supply-Health and Welfare defence. It is also the practice being followed in the United States, a country comparable for our present purpose in governmental structure to our own. As the leader of the opposition knows, so far as financial responsibility is concerned, even during the war the municipal organizations and local governments in the United Kingdom continued to bear a very heavy portion of the cost of civil defence. There were co-ordinating plans issued and general direction given by the central government, but the purchase of civil defence equipment, the stockpiling of material and the like in the United Kingdom were done, as we are doing it, on a share for share basis. We do regard this matter as important. It is difficult, I may say frankly, to determine the full extent to which we should go; and in this matter we are guided not only by our own appreciations of the temper of the world at this time but also by the consultative arrangements we have with the ten provinces who with the federal government constitute the civil defence committee of this country.
We met with all the provinces about six weeks ago in this building and reviewed what had been done and what it was proposed to do during the ensuing year. I would not say that we were in agreement on all counts, but the following quotation from the Edmonton Journal of May 7, in which the minister in charge of civil defence for the province of Alberta expressed his view of the conference, sets out, I think, better than anything I can say the measure of understanding between ourselves and the provinces. Mr. Gerhart is reported to have said:
Although differences of opinion still exist between the federal and the Alberta governments "better understanding than ever before" of the problems of civil defence was shown at the Ottawa meetings. The minister was hopeful that existing problems now slowing defence co-ordination could be cleared up soon.
Our conception of the problem is this. If a civil defence organization has to be employed, civil defence cannot be done here in Ottawa or in any provincial capital alone, but on the local level. Civil defence is essentially a local matter; it is comparable to the role of the good citizen coming to the aid of his neighbour through voluntary action; and if you have not developed an adequate local organization nothing that is done at the centre will be fully effective. Proceeding on that principle the provinces and ourselves have arrived at a division of responsibility somewhat as follows. We are responsible for certain phases of activity, notably training and the provision of training equipment. The provinces are responsible for setting up their provincial civil defence organizations and,
[Mr. Martin.l
through them in most communities under their jurisdiction, a civil defence organization with a civil defence director at the head.
Every community in Canada of any size now has a civil defence director; they come directly, in the scheme of organization, under the minister of civil defence for the provinces; for instance, in the province of Ontario, the provincial secretary. At the centre we are responsible for the training of the individuals whose job it is to carry on the training schools and to build up the local organizations. For instance, at our local school at the Connaught Ranges here in Ottawa we have in the past year and a half trained some 1,600 people. We have brought these individuals from all parts of Canada, paid their expenses while here, their travelling expenses, and so on. Those men and women have gone back to their local communities and have either taken jobs as civil defence co-ordinators or have fitted themselves into the local organization in one way or another.
This is an impressive record. I think that training is a basic requirement, because unless you have people who have some conception of what civil defence is all about you cannot carry on the effort at the local level.
In addition the federal government has the responsibility for publication of manuals, production of displays and films that are being used to train leaders and to bring home to the people the desirability of taking part in the civil defence organization. We have undertaken, and we have carried out this undertaking, to. give to the provinces and through them to the municipalities concerned all kinds of training equipment including, for instance, such things as coveralls, helmets, respirators, stirrup pumps and certain kinds of other material. Those are outright grants or gifts, purchased by us and given to the provinces for the purpose of building up their local organizations.
In addition we have entered into an arrangement with the St. John Ambulance Corps for the training of civil defence workers in first aid. As the leader of the opposition has said, this is an important phase of civil defence training. Normally the St. John Ambulance Corps would train about 55,000 people a year in first aid activity. We hope that in the ensuing period they will be able to train some 132,000 people in first aid. We are paying them on an agreed basis to carry on that work.
In addition we have established here our own advance warning communication system, independent of the armed forces, and

independent of the normal systems of communication utilized by the civil arm of government. We have established an advance warning communication system that will be for the exclusive use of the civil defence organization. When I discussed this particular matter in the house before, I indicated that I could not go into details and the hon. member for Nanaimo was kind enough to take advantage of the invitation I then issued to discuss privately with me the particulars of that system.
In addition to our responsibility for the things I have been talking about in a general way, equipment for training, maintaining, and -our responsibility for manuals, films and so on, we will now enter into a matching arrangement in respect of certain phases of the program which a year ago we were not prepared to recognize as a federal responsibility. This matching arrangement will provide that the federal government will pay 50 per cent of any project in which a province wishes to participate. We discussed this matter at the conference six weeks ago and we have great expectations that certain undertakings, which we consider in the long term to be matters of special interest to the provinces but have an indirect civil defence value, may be carried out.
I wish to indicate now that I would not want to say or to have anyone say that if this country were subjected to an attack such as the hon. gentleman has envisaged, we would have an adequate civil defence organization. I would be the last man to claim that. This is not the case, nor is it the case with Sweden, the United States, the United Kingdom or any other country where obviously there must be a very intimate interest in this problem at this time. What I want the country to know, and what I am sure my hon. friend would want me to say, is that there is a very considerable amount of civil defence activity going on in Canada. Every city that we conceive to be of possible significance as a target area has a civil defence director. We estimate now that there would be about 60,000 civil defence workers in Canada. Cities like Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Montreal, Windsor, and Halifax are well organized. In the city of Winnipeg they have about 3,500 workers; in the city of Montreal they have about 8,500 workers; and the budget of the city of Montreal for civil defence is something like $200,000 for the ensuing year.
These general observations will give, as I want them to give, ample evidence that this matter is being taken seriously. We
Supply-Health and Welfare are not at the point where one can say that we have a civil defence organization that by any stretch of the imagination will take care of the needs that might conceivably arise. I do not suppose any nation will ever be able to claim that; because in the kind of warfare that we must envisage, if it should ever come, as the leader of the opposition has said and I do not disagree, we have to realize the inevitability of a certain amount of risk.
I want the house and the leader of the opposition to know that the general plans of the provinces and ourselves are now sufficiently developed to justify what Sir John Hodsoll said, namely that on a comparative basis civil defence preparations in this country are comparable with those of any other country. Sir John Hodsoll has had the opportunity of sitting in on the meetings with the ten provinces. He has visited the entire country. As a matter of fact, he has been visiting again this week with the mayors of our country, along with General Worthington, at the mayors' conference in Calgary.
I want to thank the leader of the opposition for the well deserved tribute he paid to the civil defence director in Canada, who is carrying on this very difficult task with singular success.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that the general situation which obtains in the world at the present time requires that we should make some study of the financial affairs of our nation. I should therefore like to make a few remarks. 1 do not expect the minister to take the time to make any comment upon what I have to say unless he so desires this afternoon.
I realize that we have not as much time at our disposal as we should like to have. It is a most regrettable thing that the estimates of the Department of Finance, the most important estimates in the nation, should have to come in at the time these are coming in.
I am not implying that there is any fault on the part of the minister, but that fact does not in any way detract from the importance of these estimates. The balance wheel of the whole economy of the nation is its finance department.
I do not have nearly so much feeling of concern about the minister's department since the passing of the bill recently by which the Bank of Canada Act was amended so as to make it practically certain that no gold entered into the consideration of Canada's money. I have contended for 17 years in the House of Commons that the only real backing of money is, and ought to be, goods and services, quite regardless of the amount of gold we may or may not have.
On June 26 I laid down four principles which, in my judgment, are essential in a realistic financial system. On that occasion I defined a realistic financial system as one which could make what is physically possible, financially possible. As soon as one realizes that the justification for finance is physical reality in respect of goods, then one understands my principle that whatever is physically possible, it ought to be possible to make financially possible. I therefore once more lay down the four principles essential for a realistic financial system, namely, a system that could make what is physically possible financially possible.
The first principle is that the value of money depends upon goods and services, a statement which was tacitly agreed to, by the passage of the bill, by the Department of Finance. The second is that debt-free money, under certain circumstances, can be created by a state soundly, and used safely in the conduct of the financial and economic affairs of the nation. The third one is that granted adequate production, the use of debt-free money in establishing and maintaining stabilized prices throughout the nation is entirely feasible. The fourth principle is that the use of debt-free money to supply purchasing 55704-2713s
Supply-Finance
power to consumers in order to enable them to buy the production of a nation is completely sound and should be so recognized.
In connection with this fourth principle, may I lay down a certain modification. On June 26 I was contemplating only the financing of the consumption of goods and services within the nation. It also is true, in connection with a realistic financial system, that debt-free money can be created by a state for the financing of consumption outside that state, under suitable circumstances. I have illustrated that fact several times already this year by referring to what occurred in world war I when the finance department printed $50 million worth of bills, and purchased $50 million worth of wheat and lent it to Great Britain for a number of years. In that case the debt-free money mechanism was used to finance consumption outside the nation.
To sum up, not only can this debt-free money be used to produce markets within the nation but it can be used to produce markets to finance consumption outside the nation. This modification is of the utmost importance in the particular age in which we live. I hope to elaborate on that matter to a certain extent in the remarks which I shall make, and I hope they will not be unduly long.
There are two kinds of export markets that we need to finance. First of all, there is the market in which we are going to deliver goods-sell them if you wish to call it that-to nations which do not have the wherewithal to pay us, as for example the hundreds of millions of people who today dwell in Asia who have no means whatsoever whereby to repay us in goods, services or in any other form whatsoever. These people constitute an excellent market if we can only determine the means whereby to furnish them with purchasing power.
Then we have the class of market found in a nation which is able to return to us goods which we, for some reason or other, are unable to accept. We would find an example of that sort of market in Great Britain. Great Britain can consume almost unlimited quantities of our surplus production, but when she comes to send us textiles or other British production in order to repay us, then for reasons which we consider good, we do not feel that it is advisable to accept those goods and to allow them to come into competition with our own production in our own country and thus to distort our own economy. We therefore find that we have two kinds of export markets in which to finance the consumption of our surplus production.

Supply-Finance
I maintain that this principle of financing export markets is of major importance in the world as we see it around us today. In fact, I think there is no other possible democratically safe solution to the problem of distribution in the world, as it is at present constituted, at least in the years in which we are now living.
Among the strangest things that I have encountered during the days that have been going by are speeches like the one that was recently given by Mr. Graham Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada, down in eastern Canada in which he condemned trade curbs. Knowing Mr. Towers as I know him, I find myself completely astounded that such a speech as that should have emanated from him at all. Our Minister of Finance has been down in the United States giving the people there a lecture about the necessity of loosening up their trade restrictions and of allowing our goods to come into their economy. Knowing the minister as I know him, I can hardly imagine that, without some high motive or other, he would make such remarks as that in a neighbouring country. I understand that our Secretary of State for External Affairs has gone down to the United States and said the same kind of thing to the American people, indicating that they should loosen up their restrictions and allow our goods to come into their economy, in competition with their own goods.
The United States are simply not going to do that! The sooner we recognize that fact, the sooner we shall be ready to look to something else. It is just utterly foolish for us to expect the United States to allow Canadian goods like cheese, and other things that we want to send to the United States, to go in there when they do not need those goods.
I think I will quote a few passages from a good article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of May 2, 1952. It is called "The Paradox of U.S. Trade Bars", by Michael L. Hoffman, New York Times Service. From it I read as follows:
Geneva.
It was an essential part of the Marshall plan that Europe should earn its way by increasing production and selling abroad more of what its farms and factories produce.
And further in the article I read:
The United States said it would not use quotas to restrict imports and objected to other countries doing so except in emergencies to protect their monetary reserves. The United States said it would simplify its customs laws, which often exclude goods for capricious reasons.
By 1951 Europe had increased sales to the United States by about 30 per cent. All of Europe's exports to the United States, however, still amounted to a paltry $100 million a month-1/230 of our monthly national income.

And further on:
After five years of promises by the administration, congress still has not passed any customs simplification law. The United States has not joined the ITO. Unilaterally and in violation of the general agreement on tariffs and trade, the United States slapped quotas on imports of cheese, milk products and casein, thus at one blow crippling the major dollar-earning industries in Italy, Denmark, The Netherlands, Norway and New Zealand.
Since mid-1950 the axe has fallen on fur-felt hat bodies, almonds and cheese. In the form of hearings under the so-called "escape clause" in the American reciprocal trade law-which authorizes the tariff commission to raise duties if it finds that the domestic manufacturer has been seriously injured by competition-the axe is now hanging over motorcycles, bicycles, wines, pottery, "blue cheese," tobacco, pipes and wood screws.
The article goes on:
The feeling in Europe is this: If, under one kind of escape clause or another, United States producers are to be guaranteed that any product which proves itself marketable in the United States behind a protective wall high enough to overcome the difference in European and American costs, Europe will never be able to earn enough dollars to enable it to enter fully into a trading community with the United States based on a principle of non-discrimination.
From the European point of view the root of the problem is the American belief that it is right and necessary to exclude products of "cheap labour". If products of labour that is "cheap" in dollar terms (meaning that it would be cheap if it were in the United States) are to be kept out, Europe does not have a chance.
And I might say not only does Europe not have a chance, but neither does any other country in the world. This is a most revealing article, a most frank and honest statement of the situation exactly as it is in the year of our Lord, 1952, the year we happen to be living in. If there is anyone reckless enough, in the face of an article like that and in the face of the realities that support that article, to imagine for one minute that the United States is going to loosen up her trade restrictions to permit enough goods to come in from the outside to obtain dollars which the nations need with which to buy United States produce, all I can say is that he is far more of an optimist and probably more of an unrealist than really should be running at large nowadays.
May I just give a few more bits of evidence to indicate the small possibility that the United States will contemplate bringing in goods from abroad. The United States wants to sell goods. She does not want to buy unless it be raw materials. When she is able to sell the goods she is able to produce she is able to give markets to her own producers; she is able to give jobs to her own people. Above all other things, the object of the United States today is to find jobs for her people. Roosevelt said in a broadcast in October, 1944: "I mean to find jobs for 60 million Americans by tripling our exports abroad."

Notice he did not say a word about imports, and he did not mean a word about imports. Neither have said or meant the realistic men who have succeeded him in office in the United States.
Here is some more evidence of the growing self-sufficiency of the United States. The United States self-sufficiency is the major single factor in the world today. I am citing some information that I gathered in the December, 1949, issue of the Reader's Digest. This article has to do with the scarcity of United States dollars. It deals with the various commodities which the United States used to import, but which in recent years she has learned to manufacture substitutes for, or to manufacture herself. The first one of importance is cryolite. It used to be bought from Greenland, a colony of Denmark, which country used to use the American dollars from cryolite to buy United States machines. The United States in world war II manufactured synthetically her cryolite. It has almost displaced the Greenland product. Since before world war I the United States have developed synthetic sodium nitrate plants at Muscle Shoals, Alabama and Hopewell, Virginia, nitrate identical with that coming from Chile which used to provide the United States with nitrogen fertilizer. For Chile's sake only, the United States agrees not to operate some government plants. Any moment the United States may decide to manufacture all the nitrates she needs.
Before 1913 the United States bought 26,000 tons of dyes a year, making herself only
3,000	tons. By 1923 nine-tenths of the United States consumption was United States made, with 18 million pounds over for export. By 1939 the United States was making 1,000 different kinds of dyes with production equal to Germany's. By the end of world war II she had captured all of Germany's dye secrets. This was one of the difficulties that stood in the way of Germany in her attempts to recover industrially. It stands in her way today in any attempt to recapture her markets.
Let us take rubber. In 1940 the United States purchased 1-8 billion pounds of crude rubber. Four years later she was making 2 billion pounds of synthetic rubber. In 1939 the United States imported from India 95 per cent of dll the mica she used. Today United States makes its own mica by a formula seized from Germany-one more difficulty for Germany. The United States used to import all of its camphor from Formosa. In 1933 the United States began making camphor from turpentine, and now she makes more than she can use. Another difficulty for China, you see. Thirty-five years ago all the United States optical glass and instruments came from Germany, France
Supply-Finance
and England. They are now all produced in the United States. Cigarette papers used to come from France made by her from linen rags by a secret process. Now they are all made in the United States by a secret process from flax fibre, and $10 million of United States dollars are therefore denied to France.
As regards silk, between 80 million pounds and 90 million pounds a year used to come from Japan. Nearly $500 million a year was the cost. It is now made in the United States as nylon from coal, air and water. Soybeans used to come from Manchuria. Now United States farmers produce over 200 million bushels a year. Her sugar could now all be produced from sugar beets in America, whereas Americans used to import a very great deal from abroad.
Figs used to come from abroad. Now in the southwestern states over 60 million pounds of figs are produced in a year. Dates, prior to 1920, all came from North Africa and the Middle East, but now the United States produces around 20 million pounds yearly in the deserts of southern California and Arizona. Tungsten used to be imported from China or Bolivia but the United States is now using molybdenum, of which they have a whole mountain in Colorado. She now produces her own. Shellac used to come from India but now it is made from synthetic resin and corn glutens. Jute for burlap used to come from India. Now the United States has a substitute made from long-fibre spruce. And so the list goes on.
It is quite obvious that the United States is becoming more and more self-sufficient and will continue to become more and more selfsufficient as her knowledge of scientific techniques increases and the inventive genius of her people evolves new substances made from the things they already have. In the face of this fact, and others which I could adduce to bring us up to date, how can any realistic individual persuade himself into imagining that the United States is ever again under normal conditions going to be to any great extent a market for any outside nation?
The question is: What are we going to do about this situation? Here are the realities that face us. What are we going to do about them? We certainly cannot rely on trade where we have to depend upon the United States as being a partner in that trade. At the same time, we can rely upon having United States competition pressing into our very vitals in every market of the world including our own. Once more I ask: What are we going to do about it? I do not expect the minister to answer this question, but I am asking the question for those who read

Supply-Finance
Hansard and the other members of the house to answer. If you were the Minister of Finance, what would you do about that? You cannot go on as we have done. It is just absurd, because you face a situation utterly new.
What is the United States herself going to do about it? We cannot solve her problems, but I will venture to say that if the United States used her constitutional power to have congress create money debt-free as Lincoln did to represent the surplus goods which she has to sell in the world and she sent those created dollars away to the nations within whose borders she desired to sell her products she would have no difficulty whatsoever in disposing of her surpluses and her producers would be just as well off as though they had received the money of that particular nation in return for what had been sent abroad.
This is a point of extreme importance. Those who have not read "The United States in the World Economy", an official United States document published in 1943 and which is available in our library, will do well to read it and find out how the United States financed her exports abroad between 1918 and 1928 by loans to the nations which would be the prospective buyers of her goods. We know also how under the Marshall plan the United States has financed the consumption of her goods abroad. We know that she has now another act, the name of which I never can recall, under which she is sending abroad .great sums of money with whieh the people who receive that money will buy United States goods. Thus the United States is already established and is carrying on quite successfully a method of financing the consumption of her goods by sending money abroad to buy those goods.
Surely that indicates the line along which the solution lies. No nation would be able to tax its people for enough money to lend abroad for people to buy its goods. No nation could afford to go into debt to get money to send abroad. But nations like the United States and Canada certainly could create money debt-free in so far as they had surplus goods and send that money abroad.
There is one further aspect of this matter to which I think we should give some attention. Those who have read the Economic Review, a periodical issued by the United Kingdom information office in Ottawa, will have been impressed by an article in the current issue entitled, "Trade, not Aid." The British do not want aid from abroad. All they want is trade. But we cannot trade with them nor can the United States because when either of us takes their goods into our economy they compete with our own and put

our own producers out of business, throwing a lot of our people into the unemployed lists. No realistic administration could tolerate that sort of thing.
What are we going to do for Britain to let her have trade and not aid? Why not say to Britain, "Prepare us all the goods that you feel you would like to send us to buy goods from Canada that you might desire, and we will accept ownership of those goods in Britain." We would not promise to let them come into Canada to compete with our own producers, but we would accept the goods to cancel off the debt. If we deliver a million dollars worth of goods to Great Britain and they produce and deliver for us a million dollars worth of goods, we would accept ownership of those goods in Britain. Where they go from there would be another matter.
We are a partner in the Colombo plan. What we are doing under that plan is just small change, but the plan is a fine idea. We could be distributing goods and services to the various members of the commonwealth for the benefit and blessing of the people of the commonwealth. Why not take that million dollars worth of goods which Britain would have produced and delivered to us to pay for a million dollars worth of products of various kinds that she has obtained from us, and have them distributed under the Colombo plan?
If we create a million dollars worth of debt-free money in Canada and buy a million dollars worth of our own cheese for example in Canada, the dollars which the producers receive would be just as good as solid gold or the money they would get if the cheese were sold in the best market in the world. If we sent Britain a million dollars worth of cheese or let her have a million debt-free dollars to buy cheese, that cheese would be delivered to Britain which would bless Britain. Then if we enabled her to produce a million dollars worth of textiles or other goods to pay for that cheese and have those goods come into our possession in Britain, we would have been repaid. Then we could say to Britain, we wish you to send those goods to Sierra Leone or South Africa or Ceylon or India, or any other part of the empire. By doing that we should greatly bless the recipients of those goods and greatly bless Britain because we should have enabled her to maintain her prosperity and self-respect.
Can anyone find anything wrong with that device or suggestion? Now, the United States could similarly accept payment for as many exports as she might see fit to produce and

export for the next fifteen or twenty years, and even beyond that. This illustrates the value that could accrue to us in these perilous times in which we are living by the use of the debt-free money device to finance the consumption of our goods abroad.
There is one more step which I have suggested in times past and which I am going to suggest once more for the minister's serious consideration. I am quite heartened by the move he has made in respect of the Bank of Canada. I feel that the minister and his department are progressing right along. All they have to do is grow a little faster and we shall make still more progress. May I suggest then once more what 1 have suggested already. Why not let Britain be the distributing centre? There are no people on the face of the earth who know more about the goods which the various parts of the empire and in fact the world itself produce or need. Why not let Britain use the great knowledge and experience she has of trade channels, and those extensive trade connections which she has built up over the centuries to distribute these goods in accordance with the needs of the commonwealth and then the needs of people outside the commonwealth? Why not let Britain use the pound sterling when she begins to distribute these goods? As far as I have been able to find, no monetary unit has been more successful than the pound sterling backed by British production in the hands of Great Britain during the last half century. Why not let her expand the pound sterling and by means of the pound sterling bring in the things from other countries that they can supply her and return to them the goods they need from her own supply, these supplies being greatly augmented and supplemented by imports from everywhere and contributions from Canada and other members of the commonwealth? Let Britain, greatly strengthened by all of this, distribute goods abroad.
I submit that the suggestion I have made this afternoon constitutes the answer to an extremely important situation facing the world at the present time. Before taking my seat I wish to read certain quotations from a speech of the Prime Minister, who has been making some forward-looking speeches recently. I notice he is here in the chamber and has been paying close attention to what 1 am saying. I think it was in Montreal-he will correct me if I am wrong-that he made a speech indicating the great things that were ahead of this country by reason of the discovery of atomic energy. Let me say to the Prime Minister that while that speech was full of vision and understanding it will

not do a bit of good to increase our productive capacity through atomic energy if we cannot sell our goods. The Prime Minister will understand that fully. The world will only be worse off as the result of discovery of atomic energy if it increases its productive capacity without learning how to distribute.
I wish to read one or two passages from a speech the Prime Minister delivered on January 22, 1952, at the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Montreal. There are a number of passages in the speech which would reward consideration, but I am only going to quote two. He said:
I doubt if we can ever hope for the secure peace in the world which we all want so much as long as great numbers of people are barely able to eke out an existence bordering on, or in many cases below, the subsistence level.
Further on he says:
I realize of course that there are serious problems of distribution as you were reminded by your president this morning.
The Prime Minister had nothing to say about what might be the solution to those problems. That is the thing the world wants. What is your solution? Further on the Prime Minister used these words:
It has been ably stated that "never before has the close relationship between food and peace, food and justice, and food and human happiness been so widely accepted."
These words do the Prime Minister great honour. May I submit to him that if he equips himself so that one year from the date on which he delivered that speech he can go before that same organization and tell it how to distribute these goods he will be the outstanding man of the world and the world will recognize him as such. I submit what I have said this afternoon may give the Prime Minister something to think about as he prepares to deliver such a speech.

['The minister will understand that it was not about the amount but rather the manner in which these items are brought in at the very last, when the membership of the house is depleted, that I was complaining. Such large amounts should be given more careful consideration.']

I want to raise a point with the minister that could involve a lot of time but as far as I am concerned I am going to do it briefly. It is a very simple question. We are members of the Bretton Woods agreement. We have subscribed and we are also interested in the world bank. I am not one of those who join the hue and cry against Bretton Woods at all, but I am concerned about their position. They seem to be drifting into the position of someone who is on the sidelines watching what is going on rather than taking part, and I would be glad if the minister would say a word or two as to what he feels the position is there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that I can quite agree that we are in a position on the sidelines. We have been forced, as the result of

circumstances with which the hon. member is thoroughly familiar, to notify the fund, and we did so in September of 1950, that we were no longer able to maintain a fixed parity for our currency unit. We are still members, and the only point I want to make is this. One realizes very well the multiplicity of reasons that have to a very considerable extent frustrated the expectations of seven or eight years ago. I read Mr. Ilsley's speech of December, 1945, just the other day. Among other things he pointed out the advantage of the organization in providing a meeting place where views could be exchanged. It seems to me at the moment that the situation is so full of difficulty that one does wish that somehow they could adopt a more positive attitude. For example, all they had to say to Great Britain in her difficulties was to suggest that she should do away with her restrictions. I do not suppose there is anyone in this house who would like to see restrictions done away with more than I would, but that did not seem to me to be very practical advice, and one just wonders whether they are sitting in an ivory tower.

Before this passes I wonder if the Minister of Finance would draw to the attention of the Minister of Transport a matter which I think is of very great importance. My attention was called to it just a day or two ago by a short editorial which appeared in the June 5 edition of the Herald-Tribune

Supply-Transport
of the town of Grande Prairie. The heading is "Let's Be Consistent":
By a near-miracle, a youthful Sexsmith pilot escaped death last week when his plane catapulted to earth as he was attempting a landing on a farm field on the edge of Grande Prairie.
Soon after the accident, Department of Transport officials were on the scene to investigate.
It doubtless won't appear in the findings but the fact is the Department of Transport is fundamentally to blame for the circumstances which set the stage for last week's accident.
Why did the group of Grande Prairie and district men owning the Aeronca figuring in the crash find it necessary to base their plane in a farm field in the first place?
The reason, pure and simple, is that the rates the Department of Transport charges for hangar space or even parking space at its airports places a heavy additional financial burden on owners of private light aircraft.
At the Grande Prairie airport, which is controlled by the Department of Transport, it costs a light aircraft owner $10 or $11 a month to park his plane outside the hangar. Rental for space inside the hangar ranges between $25 and $30 monthly.
It is costly enough to operate and maintain a light aircraft.
It is nonsense for the Department of Transport, by its rental scale, to drive these light planes from properly-equipped airports to hazardous, makeshift landing strips in country fields.
The policy is all the more nonsensical when one considers that, in Grande Prairie's case, hangars at the airport are standing idle and empty except for the rare occasion when one or two visiting light planes are placed in storage overnight.
A policy which is at once discouraging private flying and making it more hazardous is all the more difficult to understand alongside the federal government's avowed intention to do everything possible to train young pilots. The importance the government places on training air-minded young Canadians as pilots is pointed up by its policy of making a $100 grant to every man who obtains his private pilot's licence at an approved flying school.
In the interests of consistency, as well as for the welfare of Canadian aviation, the government should review a policy which is driving private pilots to country fields and setting the stage for accidents with the near tragic consequences of the mishap here.
That is the end of the short editorial. The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that a young pilot hit a power line and his plane crashed. It is the greatest miracle that he was not killed. This matter has been found of such interest generally that I notice the October, 1951, edition of the magazine Aircraft contains certain letters to the editor complaining about the same situation. I am not going to take time to read this particular letter over the signature of J. H. Dalen of Grande Prairie. I shall just point out these one or two facts. Mr. Dalen points out that the hangar at Grande Prairie airport is never heated, the water and lights are turned off, the roof leaks causing the formation of ice on aircraft parked inside during a spring thaw; the doors are never closed which results in snow blowing in and covering 90 per cent of the floor space. Then he goes on to suggest that these small private planes are

required to pay excessive charges. As a consequence they find parking space in farmers' fields some distance from the airport.
In the same magazine, Aircraft, I find an editorial on page 106 that refers to the same situation. I know something about the hangar at Grande Prairie airport. I would ask the Minister of Transport to investigate that matter and see if it would not be possible to do two things: First, to have the hangar put into good shape, repair the roof and see that the doors are made tight and are properly hanging on their hinges; second, to see if it would not be possible to arrive at a more moderate scale of rental for private planes when they are parked in the hangar of an airport.
